catalogTitle: עשה לך רב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah left its measures vague so that a Jew must keep turning to a rav and so cleave to talmidei chachamim, his main advice for holding on in the trials of emunah before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the advice for the trials before Moshiach: make yourself a rav and cling to rebbeim and good friends, as the best talmidim of Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz did. Faith in the sages is part of emunah, as the passuk joins faith in Hashem with faith in Moshe. He brings the Gemara that the seven species praising Eretz Yisrael teach the Torah's shiurim, shows that nearly every halachah depends on them, and how unclear they are. The Torah left them vague so that a Jew must keep coming to the rav and cleave to talmidei chachamim. Turning to today's trial of emunah, he explains through the word 'tevel' that the world is dark and confused, lit only by flashes. He tells stories of hidden insight from Slonim and of the Yeshuos Yaakov, and closes that one sees wonders today by reflecting on the Jews in Eretz Yisrael.

en: In the trials before Moshiach, the Mashgiach says, one of the main pieces of advice is to make oneself a rav and to stay close to rebbeim and good friends.
Just as one must believe in Hashem, one must believe that the sages of each generation are His messengers to lead the Jewish people.
Almost every halachah in the Torah depends on shiurim, measures learned from the seven species, yet those measures are far from clear.
The Torah did not give exact measures so that a Jew would constantly have to go to the rav, and through this cleave to talmidei chachamim.
Today's trial of emunah is that open wonders are rare; the world is 'tevel', a confused darkness lit only by Hashem's occasional flashes.
Even now one can see wonders by reflecting on current events, above all the survival of the Jews in Eretz Yisrael among their enemies.

title.en: Make yourself a rav: faith in the sages

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the advice for the trials before Moshiach: a rav, rebbeim and good friends, and tells how the good bochurim clung to Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz. He explains that faith in the sages is part of emunah and brings the passuk of the seven species in Parshas Eikev.

title.en: The seven species teach the shiurim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that the seven species are mentioned for the Torah's measures and goes through them, then shows how nearly every mitzvah depends on shiurim and how far apart the opinions are, such as the Chazon Ish and Rav Chaim Naeh. A house built with two different shiurim would come out crooked.

title.en: Why the Torah left the measures vague

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah, given to a people who could build with precision, measured by the hand and finger. He answers that the Torah wants a Jew to keep coming to the rav, cleaving to talmidei chachamim, until the chacham becomes his guide in all of life.

title.en: Tevel: a confused world lit by flashes

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes today's trial of emunah: there are great tzaddikim but few open wonders. He explains the world's name 'tevel' from Rashi as a confusion, like a dark night in the country, and says that even in hester panim Hashem's lightning flashes light up the confused world.

title.en: Stories from Slonim: the beard and the knife

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells stories he heard from a Slonimer chassid and others: the Slonimer Rebbe, the Beis Avraham, in Yerushalayim, who taught a shaven simple Jew and a learned chassid the difference between them, and the Rebbe's gabbai who knew that a new knife had not been toiveled.

title.en: The Yeshuos Yaakov's cake; wonders today

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells from seforim how the Yeshuos Yaakov delayed the brachah on a cake with long pilpulim until it turned out to be forbidden, and how he denied it was ruach hakodesh. He closes that today emunah is demanded, and that one sees wonders by reflecting on the Jews in Eretz Yisrael.

catalogTitle: ביאור ברייתא בסוף מס' סוטה בענין עיקבתא דמשיחא

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach goes through the baraisa at the end of Sotah on the signs of the 'heels of Moshiach', shows each sign in his own time, and concludes that with no true leaders left a Jew can rely only on his Father in Heaven and must hold fast to emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the baraisa at the end of Sotah describing the time before Moshiach and applies its signs one by one. Chutzpah grows; prices rise even when supply is plentiful; the government turns to heresy, which he sees in the Russian state, whose seventy-year atheist rule is now crumbling, illustrated by a visit to Russian Jews who had forgotten almost all of Yiddishkeit. He continues with the loss of truth, the mocking of those who turn from evil, the breakdown of respect within the family, and the face of the generation like the face of a dog: leaders who walk in front but look back to see what the crowd wants. A parable of the shepherd and his dog shows that the last leaders will only hold the people together. With no leader of the stature of the Chofetz Chaim, he says, a Jew relies on his Father in Heaven. A wheat merchant's parable teaches that today mitzvos are not scrutinized, so one can earn much. He closes by stressing the mitzvah of emunah.

en: The baraisa's signs of the heels of Moshiach, rising chutzpah and prices that climb despite plentiful supply, are visible in the Mashgiach's own time.
'The kingdom will turn to heresy' was fulfilled for the first time in history by the Russian state, and its collapse is a sign that Moshiach is near.
The face of the generation is like the face of a dog: the leaders walk in front but look back to see what the community wants.
When there is no leader for the whole people, a Jew must not despair, because the same Ribono shel Olam who gave the Torah is present today.
In the time before Moshiach mitzvos are not scrutinized in Heaven, so it is a time when a person can earn a great deal.
The mitzvah of emunah, which the Mashgiach has been teaching for years from the Sefer Chareidim, is a person's lifeline in the heels of Moshiach.

title.en: Chutzpah, rising prices and a kingdom of heresy

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens the baraisa at the end of Sotah on the heels of Moshiach and applies its first signs: growing chutzpah, prices that rise against the rules of supply and demand, and a kingdom turned to heresy, which he sees in the Russian state. He describes a recent visit to Russian Jews who had forgotten almost all of Yiddishkeit, and sees the breaking of that kingdom as a sign that Moshiach is near.

title.en: Truth missing, family broken, the dog's face

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues with the baraisa: impoverished border towns, the parallel Gemara in Sanhedrin where one who turns from evil is called mad, the absence of truth, and the young shaming the old, which he sees in the breakdown of the family. He explains 'the face of the generation like the face of a dog' with a man walking his dog: leaders walk in front but look back to see what the community wants, and avoid speaking about Shabbos, kashrus or Torah learning.

title.en: Shepherd and dog; leaders gone, rely on Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a parable of a shepherd who feeds his flock and a dog that only keeps it together: the last leaders before Moshiach will only hold the people together. He brings the passuk in Haazinu on 'none restrained or left', recalls the days of the Chofetz Chaim, the Gerrer Rebbe and the Chazon Ish, and concludes from the end of the baraisa that a Jew must not despair, for the same Ribono shel Olam is with him today.

title.en: The wheat merchant: no scrutiny in hard times

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a parable of a wheat merchant who was gloomy in times of plenty, when buyers inspected every grain, and cheerful in wartime, when hungry people took whatever he had. So too in the heels of Moshiach mitzvos are not scrutinized above, and one can earn much through Torah, tefillah and tzedakah.

title.en: The mitzvah of emunah: the most important point

summary.en: The Mashgiach announces that next week he will reach the most important point of the whole zman. He describes how his learning of the Sefer Chareidim with bochurim came to center entirely on the mitzvah of emunah, how former students thank him for keeping them in Yiddishkeit, and he asks his listeners to take it seriously, closing with the navi's words about emunah and Moshiach.

catalogTitle: סדרות מחוברים During ספירה - A Time for Unity Between Different Sects of Jews

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that combined sedras are the Torah's way of showing achdus among the separate groups of Klal Yisrael, that all strife grows from jealousy rooted in the moon's complaint against the sun, and why in a leap year the sedras of Sefirah stay apart.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the idea that every Jew draws from a particular letter of the Sefer Torah, which explains why people differ and why some tzaddikim are beyond imitation. Families, neighborhoods and communities mirror the Torah's words, columns, sedras and sefarim, and each Shabbos is woven from its own sedra, so sedras may not be mixed. Yet sometimes two sedras are joined: at certain times of year, before Nisan, before Tishrei, in the Three Weeks and in Sefirah, the separate groups must show ahavas chinam. Using the dispute between shlishi and shishi and the Midrash of the Yam Suf, he shows that machlokes comes from kinah, whose root is the moon's jealousy of the sun. Moshiach will end it, as hinted in Rosh Chodesh, Kiddush Levana and David and Yehonasan. A leap year, when the moon catches up with the sun, needs no combined sedras in Sefirah. He closes asking for Torah, shalom and erasing kinah.

en: Every Jew draws from a particular letter of the Sefer Torah, and people who share a root are joined as a family, a neighborhood or a community, just as letters form words, columns, sedras and sefarim.
Each Shabbos is woven from the letters of its own sedra, so sedras may not be mixed; when two are joined it is to show achdus among separate groups.
The sedras are joined at times that call for ahavas chinam: before Nisan and Tishrei, in the Three Weeks, and in Sefirah when the students of Rabbi Akiva did not show each other honor.
All machlokes and all the troubles of history come from kinah, jealousy, and kinah breeds sinah, hatred.
The root of kinah is the moon's jealousy of the sun, and when Moshiach comes the moon will be restored and kinah will be removed from the world.
A leap year, in which the moon catches up with the sun, is itself a sign of the moon's repair, so its Sefirah weeks need no combined sedras as a reminder.

title.en: Each Jew's letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that every Jew draws from a letter of the Sefer Torah, which explains differences among people. Some tzaddikim, like the Chofetz Chaim, are beyond imitation because their letter is especially holy, and a tzaddik who put all his strength into Shabbos had his root in Shabbos.

title.en: Families, neighborhoods and sedras

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a family is people whose letters form one word, three families make a neighborhood like a column, and a community is like a sedra. Each Shabbos is woven from its own sedra, so the Zohar forbids mixing sedras, and the five sefarim mirror the camps in the Midbar.

title.en: Why sedras are sometimes joined

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how two sedras can ever be read together if mixing them is forbidden. He explains that each group of Jews has its own Shabbos, customs and even halachos, as with Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel, yet at certain times unity must be demonstrated, as the shevatim gathered in Yerushalayim on Yom Tov.

title.en: Four seasons of ahavas chinam

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Beis Hamikdash was destroyed for sinas chinam, so at four times of year the sedras are joined to show ahavas chinam: before Nisan and Tishrei, the two months of hoped-for redemption, in the Three Weeks, and in Sefirah. He then asks why in a leap year the Sefirah sedras are not joined, rejecting the answer that it is only because of the extra weeks.

title.en: Chassidim and misnagdim: shlishi and shishi

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the separations of recent generations, Chassidim and misnagdim, Ashkenazim and Sefardim, and how halacha governs every movement, as the Chasam Sofer's father taught his son. He illustrates with the aliyah given to a Rav: shlishi by halacha, shishi among Chassidim following the Zohar, and on weeks of joined sedras shlishi and shishi come together.

title.en: The Yam Suf and the quarrel of shlishi and shishi

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Midrash that the sea refused to split for Moshe, since the sea was created on the third day and man on the sixth, until it saw Yosef's coffin. Hashem rebuked the sea for quarreling over shlishi and shishi while Jews were in danger, and the Mashgiach applies this to today's machlokes, which comes from jealousy.

title.en: Kinah through history and its root

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that kinah breeds sinah, from the nations' hatred of Jews to the nachash, Kayin, Yosef's brothers, Yeravam and Kamtza bar Kamtza, and tells of a tzaddik who traveled to Rav Yisrael of Vizhnitz to learn freedom from kinah. He traces kinah to the moon's complaint against the sun.

title.en: Moshiach, the moon and Yehuda and Ephraim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Yeshayahu's vision of peace among animals and the verse that Ephraim will not envy Yehuda, explaining that the moon will be restored. He lists three expressions of the moon's diminution, including its slower pace that requires a leap month, and identifies Yehuda and David with the moon.

title.en: David and Yehonasan and Rosh Chodesh

summary.en: The Mashgiach presents the love of Yehonasan for David despite Shaul's jealousy as a symbol of the end of kinah, which each month is hinted in Kiddush Levana and the haftarah of Machar Chodesh. He explains the Rosh Chodesh chatas 'for Hashem' as the promise of the moon's repair, and says the machlokes among Jews holds back Moshiach.

title.en: The leap year answer and closing

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers his question: a leap year, when the moon catches up with the sun, is itself a sign of the moon's repair, so Sefirah needs no combined sedras. He closes with Rosh Chodesh Iyar as a month of Torah, calls to erase kinah, since a Jew's deeds register in all creation like a switchboard, and expresses hope for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: זהירות בקדושה וכשרות המאכלים

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the soul, like the body, loses its healthy appetite for Torah and emunah through forbidden food and through lapses in kedushah, and he teaches how to handle the doubts in emunah that come in their wake.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach compares the soul to a living organism: just as unhealthy food ruins the body's appetite, sins dull the heart, and forbidden food above all weakens a person's emunah. He supports this with a letter of the Rambam and with the Divrei Chaim's explanation of why German Jewry fell, and warns how hard kashrus is today, urging care about whose hechsher one relies on. The second cause of doubts is a lapse in kedushas Yisrael, guarding the eyes and thoughts. He explains that before Moshiach the power of Amalek, whose gematria equals safek, grows, so many sincere bochurim suffer doubts; their pain itself shows they believe. One must not argue with such thoughts, which are leitzanus rather than logic, but push them away; the Bnei Yissaschar says this fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru'. He closes by tying this to parshas Shelach and the summer travel season as a shlichus.

en: The soul is a spiritual organism: just as bad food ruins the body's appetite, sin dulls the heart and takes away the soul's natural desire for Torah, tefillah and Hashem's will.
Of all sins, eating forbidden food in particular causes a person to lose his emunah.
Kashrus today is very difficult, so one must know that the rav giving a hechsher is both a yerei shamayim and competent in the field.
The second cause of doubts in emunah is a lapse in kedushas Yisrael, guarding one's eyes and thoughts.
Doubts in emunah before Moshiach come from the strengthening of Amalek, and a person who suffers from them is not a non-believer; his very pain shows that he believes.
One must not argue with doubting thoughts or answer them with logic; one pushes them away and ignores them, and they will pass.

title.en: Forbidden food dulls the soul's appetite

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the soul to the body: unhealthy food ruins a person's appetite for good food, and sins take away the soul's natural desire for Torah and tefillah. He brings the Gemara that sin dulls the heart and says forbidden food above all causes a loss of emunah.

title.en: The Rambam, German Jewry and kashrus today

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a letter to the Rambam about techiyas hameisim, whose answer traced the questioners' weak emunah to forbidden food, and of the Divrei Chaim's explanation that German Jewry fell because its shochtim were not God-fearing. He then describes how hard kashrus is today with packaged ingredients, and says one may rely only on a hechsher of a rav known to be both a yerei shamayim and expert.

title.en: Kedushah, doubts and the power of Amalek

summary.en: The Mashgiach names the second cause of doubts: lack of care in kedushas Yisrael, from the passuk in the week's parsha about not straying after one's heart and eyes. He says many sincere bochurim come to him in tears over doubts, explains that before Moshiach Jews will enter the fiftieth gate of impurity, and that doubts come from Amalek, which equals safek in gematria.

title.en: Doubts before Moshiach are a test, not kefirah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares today's spiritual atmosphere to physical pollution, and says the bochurim's tears over their doubts show they believe. He brings the Ohr Hameir and Reb Yisroel of Ruzhin on how hard emunah will be before Moshiach, and teaches that everyone faces such a period and should push the thought out like a fly that keeps returning.

title.en: Don't argue with the thoughts: 'velo sasuru'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man whom a tzaddik told to ignore a disturbing image during davening, and recalls his own shock as a bochur when a friend told Reb Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz he had doubts. He explains that such thoughts are leitzanus, not logic, so they must be pushed away rather than answered, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that pushing them out fulfills the mitzvah of 'velo sasuru', with a remez from its trop.

title.en: A private geulah and the summer as a shlichus

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew should await his own redemption from a period of trials and emerge from it with clearer emunah, strengthening himself in Torah and tefillah and ignoring the doubts. He contrasts the meraglim of the parsha with Yehoshua's successful spies of the haftarah, calls the summer travels a shlichus that can repair the meraglim's forty days, and parts with wishes for a successful summer.

catalogTitle: ציפוי לגאולה ועניני משיח

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that hoping and waiting for Moshiach every day, even through disappointments, is the obligation of every Jew, the tikkun of Adam's sin, and a channel for all yeshuos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a person is asked in Heaven whether he awaited the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah. He shows this hope in Shemoneh Esrei and in the Rambam's principle that one awaits Moshiach every day. In times of trouble and war the hope should be sharper, with a cheshbon hanefesh. He says the events of the Holocaust and the founding of the State were not the geulah, that Hashem runs the world by His own plan, and that the disappointments were foretold by Yeshaya as birth pangs that bring forth nothing. The Ramban on Haazinu shows that the fulfilled prophecies guarantee the rest. All galus comes to repair Adam's sin of not waiting, repeated at the Golden Calf and by Shaul, while David waited. After the Malbim's story about waiting, he shows how waiting draws down yeshuos, and how the tefillos are full of this hope.

en: Every Jew is obligated to hope constantly for the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah, as the Gemara, Shemoneh Esrei and the Rambam's principles show.
In times of trouble and war, when the signs point to Moshiach, a person should be more aroused and make a cheshbon hanefesh.
The disappointments of recent generations were not the geulah, but the navi already foretold such birth pangs that bring forth nothing.
The sin of Adam, repeated at the Golden Calf and by Shaul, was not waiting; the avodah of galus is to wait, and this repairs that sin.
By hoping for Moshiach, the root of all yeshuos, a Jew draws down personal yeshuos even now, and a Jew is measured by how much he hopes.

title.en: The question in Heaven: did you await the yeshuah?

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that a person is asked in Heaven whether he awaited the yeshuah, which includes the complete geulah. He shows this hope in the Shemoneh Esrei bracha of Es Tzemach David and in the Rambam's principle, condensed in Ani Maamin, that one awaits Moshiach every single day.

title.en: Heightened hope in times of trouble

summary.en: Although one must hope every day, the Mashgiach explains that when troubles and wars come, as Chazal describe, a person should be more aroused and ask himself whether he has learned and davened enough. He tells of Rav Moshe of Savran, who remembered every thought because for him every moment was like a wedding.

title.en: Not the geulah, and the great disappointment

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that what happened after the Holocaust and with the founding of the State was not the geulah or its beginning, but the opposite of what the Rambam describes. Hashem runs the world by His own plan, and a Jew's task is Torah and mitzvos, not politics. He describes the disappointment after the churban and after the miracles in Eretz Yisrael this year.

title.en: Birth pangs that bring forth nothing, and the Ramban on Haazinu

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Yeshaya, who compares the geulah to a birth preceded by pangs, and laments a woman who suffers and bears a stillborn child: the navi foresaw such disappointments. The end of Haazinu speaks of the geulah, and the Ramban argues that since the first part of the prophecy came true, the second part will surely come too.

title.en: Not waiting: from Adam to the Golden Calf and Shaul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that all galus comes to repair Adam's sin, which was not waiting until Shabbos, when the eitz hadaas would have become permitted. The Golden Calf was the same failure to wait for Moshe, and Shaul did not wait for Shmuel, while David waited for the sign and began the tikkun. Every Jew, a fragment of Adam, repairs his share by waiting.

title.en: The Malbim: a Jew knows how to wait

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Malbim, debating a maskil, described his morning: hungry, yet waiting through washing, davening, netilas yadayim, hamotzi and the salt before eating. From here he says the whole Shulchan Aruch is waiting, and so is Shabbos.

title.en: Waiting despite disappointment, and the joy when he comes

summary.en: Through the example of orlah the Mashgiach shows that a Jew's avodah is waiting, and that despite disappointments one keeps waiting, which repairs Adam's sin. He brings Chavakuk, Yeshaya and Tehillim on the reward of those who wait, and describes how, when Moshiach comes, Jews will point to Hashem and say this is the One we hoped for, and every minute of waiting will be a treasure.

title.en: Waiting draws down yeshuos; the power of amen

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that by waiting for the general yeshuah of Moshiach, the root of all yeshuos, one draws down healing and success even now, drawing water from its wellspring. He brings the Gemara that emunim are those who say amen: answering amen to a bracha about what one has not yet seen is belief, and Hashem stores these amens in His treasury.

title.en: Tefillos full of hope; the measure of a Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Jews never forget Yerushalayim because they know it will be rebuilt, and that Aleinu, Shemoneh Esrei, bentching and the Shabbos Kedushah are all hope and prayer for the geulah. He concludes that a Jew is measured by how much he hopes and longs for Moshiach, and that this longing itself brings the geulah closer.

catalogTitle: צורך המיוחד להדגיש אמיתיות התורה לדורנו

oneLiner.en: In a time of hester panim, when open miracles are not seen, the Mashgiach shows why the truth of the Torah rests on events an entire people witnessed: Matan Torah before millions, and a sefer Torah that described what that whole generation had seen with its own eyes.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by describing the present as a time of hester panim, when the open miracles of earlier tzaddikim are no longer seen. He brings the passuk in Devarim that asks whether any nation ever heard the voice of G-d speaking as the Jews did, and stresses that at Matan Torah the whole people, millions of men, women and children, became prophets at once; an event witnessed by so many cannot be denied. He then turns to the last mitzvah of the Torah, that every Jew write a sefer Torah. All the sifrei Torah were identical, and the generation that received them, who had been children under twenty in the wilderness, found in it the events of the forty years they had lived through, and agreed that it was true. In the last part, he cites the principle that the Torah will never be exchanged, and argues that a Torah of hard obligations would not have been accepted had it not been true.

en: The Mashgiach describes the present as a time of hester panim, when the open miracles of earlier generations are not seen.
At Matan Torah an entire people of millions heard Hashem speak and became prophets, something no other nation ever claimed.
An event that happened before so many people and was handed down through the generations cannot be denied.
Every Jew was commanded to write his own sefer Torah, and all the sifrei Torah were exactly the same.
The generation that received the sefer Torah had lived through the forty years it described and confirmed that it was true.
The Mashgiach cites the principle of faith that the Torah will never be exchanged for another.

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the last mitzvah of the Torah, that every Jew write a sefer Torah, all of them identical. The generation that received it had been children in the wilderness, recognized in it the forty years they had lived through, and agreed that it was true.

catalogTitle: Every Jew is A Letter in the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that when Moshe Rabbeinu counted the Jews 'by the number of names' he was counting the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah, so that every Jew is a letter in the Torah and the camp in the desert was itself a Sefer Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by calling the Shabbos before Shavuos the aufruf before the chuppah of Matan Torah, and turns to Parshas Bamidbar. He asks why Moshe, Aharon and the Nesi'im had to count the Jews themselves, and what 'counting names' means. Bringing the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim, he explains that the 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah: each letter carries countless halachos and secrets, and a letter that is counted is never nullified. Counting by names joins each Jew's individuality to the whole, and only leaders who know each neshama can do it. The arrangement of the camps is the arranging of the letters into a Torah; Shevet Levi, counted apart, are the 22 root letters, which is why so many teachers of Torah are Kohanim and Levi'im. The megadef was evicted because an extra letter makes a Sefer Torah pasul. He closes with stories and practical words on preparing for Shavuos, when the Torah is given anew.

en: The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf before the wedding of Matan Torah, where Har Sinai held over the people was the chuppah.
Every Jew is a letter, or part of a letter, in the Sefer Torah; there are 600,000 letters for 600,000 neshamos, and if one is missing the Torah is pasul.
Counting 'by the number of names' joins each Jew's individuality to his place in the whole, so only leaders like Moshe and Aharon, who know the secrets of each neshama, could do the counting.
Setting up the camps under flags is arranging the letters into words and pesukim, and Shevet Levi, counted separately, are the roots of the letters, the teachers of Klal Yisrael.
Every Shavuos the Torah is given anew, so one must prepare for it as for a Rosh Hashanah of Torah and not sleep through the davening and the reading.

title.en: The aufruf Shabbos before Matan Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Shabbos before Yom Tov holds the bounty of the Yom Tov, and brings the haftarah's image of Klal Yisrael as Hashem's bride, bound by emunah. Matan Torah was the wedding with Har Sinai as the chuppah, so this Shabbos is the aufruf, built from the sedra that is read on it.

title.en: Why Moshe himself counted the people

summary.en: The Mashgiach goes through the counting at the start of Bamidbar and contrasts it with the American census taker of his youth, an unemployed man sent door to door. He asks why Moshe, Aharon and the Nesi'im had to spend their time counting, and notes the repetition: a count, the Levi'im, the four camps under flags, and a recount with the same total.

title.en: Counting names; every Jew a letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what 'bemispar shemos', counting names, means, and brings the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters of the Torah, which he calls an understatement. He brings that there are 600,000 Jews like the 600,000 letters, several Jews sometimes making up one letter, and describes a scratched letter that stops the reading and renders the Sefer Torah pasul.

title.en: A letter that is never nullified

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every person present is at least part of a letter in the Sefer Torah, and that each letter carries countless halachos and secrets. The sages were called soferim because for them each letter was a davar shebeminyan, a counted thing that is never nullified, as a drop of milk is in sixty parts of soup; he ends with the sefarim's reading of the name Yisrael as the 600,000 letters.

title.en: Names, not numbers: the eyes of the congregation

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a census turns people into numbers while a family calls each child by a name that tells the secret of his neshama, and brings the Chiddushei HaRim on the prophecy given to parents at naming. Moshe's count joined the name to the number, so only leaders who know each neshama's secrets, past and future, could count; they are the 'eyes of the congregation' who see the inner glow of every Jew.

title.en: Arranging the letters into camps

summary.en: Recalling that the Aseres HaDibros contain the whole Torah, the Mashgiach explains that once the 600,000 letters were counted they had to be arranged into words and pesukim, like letters that must not be spilled on paper; this is the command to camp under flags. The five camps match the five Chumashim, with the Kohanim and Levi'im in the center as Vayikra, Toras Kohanim, is the middle Chumash, and he raises that Shevet Levi was counted separately.

title.en: Kohanim and Levi'im, the root letters

summary.en: The Mashgiach points to an open miracle: Moshe's blessing that Levi will teach Torah to Yaakov is visible in the many Kohanim and Levi'im among the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch and the leading roshei yeshiva, far beyond their tenth of a congregation. Shevet Levi are the roots of the neshamos, and their count of 22,000 corresponds to the 22 letters of the aleph-beis that are the roots of the 600,000 letters.

title.en: The megadef and the camp as a Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the episode of the man who claimed a place in the camp of Dan, lost the din Torah, cursed and was put to death, and asks why they cared in so vast a desert. He answers that the camp was Hashem's Sefer Torah, each word a family and each line a neighborhood, so an extra letter would make it pasul; he adds that the many colored flags show Klal Yisrael is many colors yet one.

title.en: Shavuos, when the Torah is given anew

summary.en: The Mashgiach says nothing requires as much preparation as Shavuos, since the Torah is given anew each year, and tells how Reb Yechezkel Shinever went to Belz for Shavuos to see the thunder and lightning of Sinai until his father, the Sanzer Rav, showed it to him at home. He compares Shavuos to Rosh Hashanah, brings a tzaddik who feared Shavuos more, and tells of the Bluzhever Rebbe, whose heart beat irregularly six days before receiving the Torah.

title.en: Don't sleep through the wedding

summary.en: The Mashgiach criticizes those who stay up all night and then doze through the davening and the Aseres HaDibros, when each Jew receives his portion in the Torah, comparing them to a chassan who sleeps through his own chuppah, and says those who cannot manage should rest a few hours first, especially for Musaf. He closes with a tzaddik's teaching that even one who missed the fifty days can recount them until the last moment of the seventh week.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches that Jewish history, read like the Megillah, reveals Hashem's hand, and he presents the 'seven wonders' of Jewish history as a way to clarify emunah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens by saying that strengthening oneself in the fundamentals of emunah requires basic knowledge, and that Hashem is seen in daily events just as in the Megillah, where every simple detail turns out to be part of the miracle; this is why the Megillah is read a second time. Jewish history is such a Megillah, as Moshe Rabbeinu says in Haazinu, 'remember the days of old'. He recalls that no other nation ever claimed a revelation to an entire people. He then describes the 'seven wonders of history' taught in Aish HaTorah courses: the eternal people, the spread of belief in one G-d, the bond to Eretz Yisrael, the return to Torah, the refusal to assimilate, the foretold hatred, and the small people that survives. He adds the Septuagint as proof the Torah text was not altered, and closes with the Torah's promises that the Jewish people will remain forever.

en: Like the Megillah, where every ordinary event turns out to be part of the miracle, all of Jewish history shows Hashem's hand once one looks back at it.
Moshe Rabbeinu told the Jews to remember the days of old and reflect on every generation, and they would see that all of history is for the sake of Bnei Yisrael.
No other nation has ever had, or even claimed, a revelation of Hashem to an entire people.
The seven wonders are each a wonder in itself, and looked at together they are all connected to one another.
The first wonder is that the Jews are an eternal people, while the great empires that ruled over them, Egypt, Bavel, Greece and Rome, have vanished.
The Septuagint, translated at the start of the second Beis Hamikdash, shows that nothing was added to the Torah later.
The Torah promises many times that the Jewish people will remain an eternal people, small in number but never destroyed.

title.en: Wonders no nation has seen; the Aish HaTorah courses

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the passuk from the week's parsha that Hashem will do wonders before the whole people, and describes the Aish HaTorah courses in Jerusalem that bring young people to teshuvah by showing them the wonders of Jewish history. He introduces their series on the 'seven wonders of history'.

title.en: The eternal people; teaching the world one G-d

summary.en: The first wonder: the Jews are an eternal people while Egypt, Bavel, Greece and Rome have disappeared. The second: the Jews brought the world to believe in one G-d, so that Christians and Muslims build on the Torah.

title.en: Wonders three through seven

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the remaining wonders: the bond to Eretz Yisrael after two thousand years, the return to Torah after the 'isms', the refusal to assimilate, the foretold hatred of the nations, and the small people that survives, illustrated by the numbers of Yishmael's and Yitzchak's descendants.

title.en: Where to begin: the eternity promised in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says each wonder needs long explanation, and that the first thing to learn is that the Jews are an eternal people, as the Torah foretold. He recalls that the whole Torah was given before all of Israel, who remembered the miracles of forty years and passed them on, so it could not have been invented later.

title.en: The Septuagint as proof

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how King Talmai had the elders translate the Torah into Greek in separate rooms, and all made the same changes, as the Gemara in Megillah relates. Since this translation from early in the second Beis Hamikdash still exists, no one can claim something was inserted into the Torah later.

title.en: The Torah's promise that Israel will remain

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that the mesorah from generation to generation cannot be falsified, and brings pesukim from Malachi, Bechukosai and Yeshayahu that the Jewish people will remain forever, small in number but eternal.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows three wonders of the Jewish people: their eternity, the nations' jealous hatred of the chosen people who light up the world, and their unique bond with Eretz Yisroel, which blooms only for them.

abstract.en: Continuing from the previous week, the Mashgiach recalls that the mighty empires that destroyed the Beis Hamikdash have vanished while the small Jewish people lives on, as the pesukim in Malachi, the tochachah, Nitzavim and Yeshayahu promise. He then asks why the nations are so bothered that Jews call themselves the chosen people, and answers that they know it is true; their jealousy turns into hatred, as the Zohar shows from Yosef and his brothers. He reads Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the Jew's immortality and a letter of President Adams on the Jews as the teachers of belief in one G-d, and adds the Abarbanel and Spain's decline after the expulsion. The third wonder is the bond with Eretz Yisroel: Jews still mourn it after two thousand years, and the land, desolate under every other people, now blooms as the Jews return, which the Gemara calls the clearest sign of the end of exile.

en: The great empires that oppressed Israel have vanished, while the small Jewish people has outlived them all, as Hashem promised through the Torah and the Neviim.
The nations hate the Jews because they are jealous of them, and they are jealous because they know the Jews really are the chosen people.
Honest non-Jewish thinkers such as Mark Twain, Tolstoy and President Adams admitted the Jew's eternity and his role in bringing belief in G-d to the world.
The Jews are a light to the nations, bringing wisdom and emunah to the whole world, as Yeshayahu foretold.
No other people longs for a land it left so long ago; the Jews still mourn Eretz Yisroel after two thousand years of exile.
Eretz Yisroel is fruitful only when the Jews are there; under others it stayed desolate, and its blooming today is the Gemara's clearest sign of the end of exile.

title.en: The eternal people outlives the empires

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls last week's theme, that the empires who destroyed the Beis Hamikdash vanished while Israel lives on, and brings the promises of Malachi, the tochachah, Nitzavim and Yeshayahu that the Jews will remain a small but enduring people and return to their land.

title.en: Why the nations hate the chosen people

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why it bothers the nations that Jews call themselves chosen, when other peoples' boasts are only laughed at. He answers that they know it is true and cannot become Jews themselves, so they are jealous, and jealousy breeds hatred, as the Zohar learns from Yosef and his brothers; this is the root of the persecutions throughout the exile.

title.en: Mark Twain and Tolstoy on the eternal Jew

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads, in English, Mark Twain's description of the Jew who is barely one percent of mankind yet outlived Egypt, Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, and Tolstoy's words that the Jew is the emblem of eternity whom no persecution could destroy. He concludes with Moshe Rabbeinu's words that the nations will call Israel a wise and understanding people.

title.en: Surviving every catastrophe; the Abarbanel and Spain

summary.en: The Mashgiach lists the catastrophes since those writers, the pogroms, the Holocaust and the wars, which the Jews survived as the eternal people and a light to the nations. Every king had Jewish advisors; the Abarbanel, minister of the king of Spain, refused to stay when the Jews were expelled, and Spain sank into insignificance without its Jews.

title.en: A light to the nations: President Adams's letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Christianity and Islam both come from the Jews, who brought emunah to the world, as Yeshayahu said that nations will walk by Israel's light. He reads a letter of President John Adams answering a call to make Jews second-class citizens, that the Hebrews did more to civilize mankind than any nation by teaching belief in one supreme G-d, and notes that Jews still fill the highest offices, fulfilling the blessing to Avraham.

title.en: The third wonder: longing for Eretz Yisroel

summary.en: The Mashgiach moves to the third wonder, the bond of the Jews with Eretz Yisroel: no other people longs for a homeland it lost, yet Jews mention and mourn it three times a day. He tells of Napoleon finding Jews mourning on Tisha B'Av and saying such a people will surely return to its land, and adds that whole communities gave their lives for Hashem, which no other nation can claim.

title.en: A land that blooms only for the Jews

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Torah's praise of the good land the Jews were brought to, and the tochachah's warning that in exile it would become desolate, so that a stranger would see it burnt and unsown. He concludes that with the Jews the land is the most fruitful, and without them a wasteland, as he himself saw on his first visit some thirty years earlier.

title.en: The blooming land as the revealed end

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes how the land, which for two thousand years no nation could settle, is now covered with fields and forests as the Jews return, and brings the Gemara in Sanhedrin that there is no clearer sign of the end than Eretz Yisroel giving its fruit. He recalls the tiny fruits once brought from there and its poverty, contrasts them with today's prosperity, and calls it a wonder before one's eyes.

catalogTitle: עריכות הפליאות יחד שייך דוקה ע”י הקב”ה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach shows that the Torah foretold Jewish history, the return of baalei teshuvah, exile, a small and hated nation that survives, and that these wonders contradict one another so that only Hashem could have put them together.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues his series on the wonders of Jewish history. Jews always kept the Torah; the idol worship found in Tanach was a powerful yetzer hara, like today's trials, not a departure from the Torah. That departure began about two hundred years ago with the Haskalah in Germany, whose destruction the Meshech Chochmah foresaw. Now, unexpectedly, a movement of baalei teshuvah has begun, a drizzle before the storm of teshuvah that will come with Moshiach, as the Torah and the prophets foretold, together with the flowering of Eretz Yisrael. He then reviews the prophecies of exile, of the Jews remaining few, and of the hatred of the nations. His central point is that these wonders contradict each other: a scattered, tiny, hated people should not survive, yet the Torah says it is eternal and a light to the nations. No human mind could foresee such a combination; only the Creator, who leads history, could.

en: The idol worship recorded in Tanach was a strong yetzer hara that people stumbled in, not an abandonment of the Torah, which began only with the Haskalah about two hundred years ago.
The rise of baalei teshuvah, unforeseen even a generation ago, fulfills the Torah's and the prophets' words that before Moshiach Jews will return and hunger to hear the word of Hashem.
The Torah foretold the exile, that the Jews would remain few among the nations, and that they would be an object of scorn among them.
These prophecies contradict one another and reason, so no historian could have predicted them together; only Hashem could foretell them.
A people scattered, tiny and hated should have disappeared like mighty Bavel, Persia, Greece and Rome, yet the Jews remain a people and even a light to the nations.

title.en: Jews kept the Torah until the Haskalah

summary.en: Returning to the wonders of Jewish history, the Mashgiach explains that the idol worship in Tanach was a strong yetzer hara, abolished by the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah, comparable to today's trials of immorality and the internet, and not a departure from the Torah. That departure began only about two hundred years ago in Germany with the Haskalah and the Reform and Conservative movements.

title.en: From Haskalah to the baal teshuvah movement

summary.en: The Mashgiach cites the Meshech Chochmah, who wrote that the Haskalah began in Germany and that destruction would begin there too, then mentions Zionism and communism. Then, some twenty or thirty years ago, a new phenomenon of baalei teshuvah began, which R' Shlomke of Zvhil foresaw; the Mashgiach notes the Lubavitcher Rebbe's strengthening of it and the fire of baalei teshuvah today.

title.en: Signs before Moshiach foretold in the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares today's teshuvah to the drizzle that precedes a storm, and ties it to the signs of Moshiach: the fruits of Eretz Yisrael that now go out to the whole world, the prophet Amos's hunger to hear the word of Hashem, and the Torah's promise in Nitzavim that Jews will return. He concludes that such foreknowledge shows the truth of the Torah.

title.en: The prophecy of exile and a remnant

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Moshe Rabbeinu's prophecy, as the Jews are about to enter Eretz Yisrael, that they will sin and be exiled, noting that the Greek translation of the Torah shows it was written long before. He cites the pesukim in Bechukosai and Va'eschanan that they will be scattered and remain few, yet will survive because Hashem leads them there, unlike the vanished great empires.

title.en: The wonder of the nations' hatred

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the hatred of the nations toward Jews, seen most starkly in the cruelty of the Germans under Hitler, and shows that the Torah foretold in Ki Savo that Israel would be an object of scorn among the nations. He repeats that the Torah also promised the Jews would remain few in number.

title.en: The wonders contradict each other

summary.en: Having gone through the wonders, the Mashgiach states the main point: they contradict one another, so reason could never connect them, and only the Ribono shel Olam could write them through Moshe and the prophets. Jewish history is unique, with no precedent a historian could extrapolate from; he frames this as one fact, A, contradicting another, B.

title.en: Eternal, scattered and hated: how can it be?

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the contradiction: no nation suffered such slaughter, and whole communities chose death over conversion, yet the Torah says the scattered few are an eternal people. He explains the hatred, citing Rashi's 'Esav hates Yaakov' and Haman's complaint that their laws differ, as the dislike of the unlike, and shows from the German Jews and Hitler that assimilation only increased it.

title.en: A light to the nations, and only the Creator foretold it

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up the contradictions and adds another: the small, hated, landless people is a light to the nations, prominent far beyond its numbers. He recalls the fruitfulness of Eretz Yisrael and tells how Ben Gurion agreed to fund yeshivos expecting them to fade, while they grew stronger. He concludes that only the Ribono shel Olam, who created and leads all, could foretell this history.

catalogTitle: The Marriage of כלל ישראל to Hashem and the תורה

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that the count of the Jews before Shavuos is the adorning of the kallah, Klal Yisrael, whose 600,000 souls are the 600,000 letters of the Torah, each with his own name and shlichus.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with a question: why did the census of Bamidbar need Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im, when a modern census uses whoever has nothing else to do? He then builds the picture of Shavuos as a wedding: Pesach is erusin, Shavuos nisuin; Hashem is the chassan and Klal Yisrael the kallah, and in a second phase Klal Yisrael is the chassan and the Torah the kallah. The 24 ornaments of a kallah are the 24 sefarim of Tanach, read on Shavuos night. The 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah, which can only be counted by knowing what each letter holds, as the aleph holds the Shem Havaya. The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf, when the kallah is counted. Counting 'by names' means each Jew has his own shlichus, which only great tzaddikim can see. He ends with how to keep Shavuos itself: not to sleep through the davening, which is the chuppah.

en: Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and also of Klal Yisrael and the Torah; Pesach is the erusin and Shavuos the nisuin.
The 24 ornaments of the kallah are the 24 sefarim of Tanach, which is why Tanach is said on Shavuos night in the Tikkun Leil Shavuos.
The 600,000 Jews correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah, and each letter is made of further letters, so counting them takes a special knowledge.
'By the number of names' means a collective made of individuals: each Jew has his own name, which is his own shlichus in the world.
The chuppah of Shavuos is the davening, especially the Kedushah of Musaf, so staying up at night and sleeping through the davening misses the purpose.

title.en: The census question and Shavuos as a wedding

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why counting the Jews needed Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im, when the United States census hires people who have nothing else to do. He then describes Shavuos as a wedding, Pesach as erusin and Shavuos as nisuin, with Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and then Klal Yisrael and the Torah, as chassan and kallah, and explains the Tikkun Leil Shavuos as preparing the kallah's 24 ornaments.

title.en: The kallah's ornaments and the Name of Adnus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Hashem as He dwells on Klal Yisrael, the kallah, is the Name of Adnus, while the Shem Havaya is beyond us; amen joins the two (26 and 65 make 91). He brings the Midrash that Hashem adorned Chava with 24 ornaments and the teaching that a talmid chacham must know the 24 sefarim, and notes that in the Tikkun Leil Shavuos each sefer is followed by one of the 24 arrangements of the Name of Adnus.

title.en: 600,000 Jews and 600,000 letters

summary.en: Recalling last week's shiur, the Mashgiach says the 600,000 Jews are the 600,000 letters of the Torah. He brings the Gemara in Kiddushin that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters, and asks why a plain count finds far fewer; the answer is that each letter contains other letters, as the aleph is made of two yuds and a vav, the gematria of the Shem Havaya.

title.en: Tzelem Elokim on the human face

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains tzelem Elokim as the human structure of 248 limbs matching the 248 positive mitzvos. On a Jew's face one sees the Shem Havaya as before the sin: the two eyes are the two yuds and the nose the vav, and the mouth beneath is a patach, chochmah, as in 'piha paschah bechochmah'; a sin takes this away.

title.en: Aliyos, Atzeres and the aufruf

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that counted properly there are 600,000 letters, and an aliyah is being called to the letters of the Sefer Torah. Shavuos and Shemini Atzeres are both called Atzeres and are both times of contact with the Torah. The Shabbos before Shavuos is the aufruf, when the Jews, the letters, are counted and the kallah is adorned.

title.en: The kallah's eyes and counting by names

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that a kallah whose eyes are beautiful needs no further checking, and explains the eyes as the Sanhedrin and nesi'im, so before the count Moshe, Aharon and the nesi'im are shown. He then explains 'bemispar shemos': mispar is a collective, shemos is individuality, and from Rashi in Vayishlach a person's name is his shlichus; people are not counted like a farmer's sheep.

title.en: Each Jew's own shlichus, and who can count

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the Nazis' numbering of Jews, meant to strip them of individuality, with Hashem's count: each Jew is a letter of the Torah with a shlichus no one else has, like the stars that Hashem calls each by name. Counting Jews this way takes great tzaddikim; he brings the Ramban that coming before Moshe to be counted brought a person merit, and explains the kvitel and the tzaddik who sees a person's purpose and earlier gilgulim, which answers the opening question.

title.en: Why Shevet Levi was not counted

summary.en: The Mashgiach places Shevet Levi in the middle of the camps, corresponding to Vayikra, the middle sefer, and asks how this fits with Levi not being counted. He explains that the extra soul of the bechor was given to the Levi'im, and that Levi is the root of Klal Yisrael, the 22 letters, which in completeness become 22,000; this reconciles the Gemara's 600,000 malachim at Matan Torah with the Midrash's 22,000.

title.en: Rabbeinu Bechaye: the degalim and the malachim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rabbeinu Bechaye, who shows that the four degalim correspond to the malachim of the Merkavah that Yechezkel saw, the four chief malachim Michael, Gavriel, Rephael and Uriel. Each degel has three shevatim, and the name of the middle nasi ends with 'el' like the name of a malach; the camp of Israel below is aimed at the camp of the malachim above.

title.en: Shavuos night and the chuppah at Musaf

summary.en: The Mashgiach sums up: the Shabbos before Shavuos the kallah is counted and her beauty shown; on Shavuos night each sefer of Tanach completed forges another golden ornament. Each year there is a new Torah, and when it is read on Shavuos a person should feel he is receiving the whole year's Torah; the chuppah itself is at Musaf, especially the Kedushah of Keser.

title.en: Not sleeping through the chuppah

summary.en: The Mashgiach warns against staying up all night and then sleeping through the holy Shavuos davening, tells of a Rebbe whose Ahavah Rabbah took two hours, and recommends that weaker people sleep three or four hours and then daven properly. He compares it to a chassan who skips the ring, and ends with the exchange at Sinai, when the upper worlds came down and Moshe went up, so on Shavuos one walks in Shamayim.

catalogTitle: הקדמה; ביאור קושיא הראשונה שבספר; ביאור כחו של שבועה.

oneLiner.en: Opening a series on Tanya, the Mashgiach introduces the sefer and its author, raises the first question of chapter one about the oath to be a tzaddik yet see oneself as a rasha, and explains why a soul is put under oath before it comes down to the world.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ba'al HaTanya, a disciple of the Maggid who excelled in the wisdom of Torah, and explains that Tanya, unlike sefarim of derashos on the parsha, sets out the foundations of Chassidus in an ordered sequence. Tanya, he stresses, belongs to all of Klal Yisrael, and he tells how Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learned it with his talmidim. Through the title page and the passuk 'ki karov', he shows that yiras Shamayim is near only by the long road. He explains the opening word 'Tanya' as breaking a klipah and as letters of the future tense, a sign of teshuvah. He then sets out the first question: the oath to be a tzaddik while seeing oneself as a rasha clashes with serving Hashem in simcha. Finally, from Avraham's oath to Eliezer, he explains that an oath releases hidden reserves of strength, and links the oath of the soul to the strength of Shabbos.

en: Tanya sets out the foundations of the Ba'al Shem Tov and the Maggid as one ordered sequence from beginning to end, not as derashos tied to the pesukim of the parsha.
The Mashgiach stresses that Tanya is the sefer of all of Klal Yisrael, learned throughout Poland and Hungary, and not the possession of one circle of Chassidim.
Yiras Shamayim is 'near' only by way of the long road; there are no shortcuts to it.
The first question of the sefer is how the oath to see oneself as a rasha fits with the need to serve Hashem in simcha.
An oath draws on a person's hidden reserves, strengths he does not know he has, for a time of emergency.
A shevuah carries the power of the seven days of creation and brings satiation and flow of blessing, which the soul needs to face the hard world.

tzaddik and rasha in one's own eyes
hidden strengths in a time of need

title.en: The Ba'al HaTanya and the order of his sefer

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces the Ba'al HaTanya as a disciple of the Maggid, greatest among them in the wisdom of Torah, and contrasts Tanya's ordered sequence with sefarim of derashos on the parsha. He notes the Ba'al HaTanya's emphasis on hisbonenus and chochmah, binah, da'as, and closes that 'these and those are the words of the living G-d'.

title.en: A sefer for all of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach says it is a great mistake to think Tanya belongs to one circle; it was learned across Poland and Hungary. He tells that Rav Shraga Feivel Mendlowitz learned it with his talmidim, explains how he will present ideas from many sefarim, and describes how the Ba'al HaTanya printed the sefer because of copying errors, gathering it from sefarim and sofrim.

title.en: 'Ki karov': the long road to yiras Shamayim

summary.en: On the passuk 'ki karov eilecha hadavar', the Mashgiach notes that yiras Shamayim is in fact very hard, as Shlomo HaMelech and the Mesillas Yesharim show. Through the Gemara's story of the short-and-long road and the long-and-short road, he explains that it is near only by the long way. He then turns to the name 'Sefer shel Beinonim'.

title.en: What learning Tanya can give

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells his listeners that the sefer can change their avodas Hashem and open the gates to other sefarim. He explains that all of Torah, including maaseh bereishis and maaseh merkavah, was given at Sinai, that only a small part of the Oral Torah remains, and that the Ba'al Shem Tov's talmidim used points of Kabbalah only where they bear on avodah, as Tanya will on a surface level.

title.en: Why the sefer opens with 'Tanya'

summary.en: The Mashgiach outlines chapter one as a chapter of questions, followed by introductory chapters before practical avodah. He discusses the Gemara in Niddah that opens with 'Tanya', brings the Zohar that a klipah bearing that name is broken by learning that begins with this word, and explains that its four letters are the letters of the future tense, as in 'Ehyeh', a sign of teshuvah.

title.en: The oath: a tzaddik who sees himself as a rasha

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the oath given to the soul, 'be a tzaddik and not a rasha, and even if the whole world calls you a tzaddik be in your eyes like a rasha', and asks how this fits with serving Hashem in simcha, which is the purpose of avodah. He shows the tension from both sides: seeing oneself as a rasha all one's life brings sadness, yet never feeling bad can lead to lightheadedness.

title.en: Why Avraham made Eliezer swear

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Avraham needed to make the faithful Eliezer swear, and likewise Yaakov with Yosef. He explains that people carry hidden strengths that emerge only in an emergency, and that Avraham knew Eliezer would face Lavan, identified with Bilaam, the head of the sitra achra. The oath would let Eliezer draw on reserves he could not otherwise reach.

title.en: What a shevuah is

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a shevuah is a great power: a person contains the whole creation, and a shevuah carries the strength of the seven days of creation. He derives the word from 'sova', satiation, and from 'shefa', since beis and peh interchange, and describes the world the soul enters as a hard place full of dangers, like a 'hall of horrors'.

title.en: The soul's oath and the strength of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that the soul, coming down from among the angels to a world of friction, needs the oath as Eliezer and Yosef did. He brings a teaching of the Slonimer tzaddikim comparing Shabbos to a warm inn for a traveler in the cold rain, and explains that the oath, like Shabbos, recharges the soul for its journey in this world.

catalogTitle: ביאור ענין מזל' האדם נברא תחת מזל - אבל לא צדיק או רשע. קושיא של איוב' בראת צדיקים בראת רשעים. ביאור מה זה צדיק.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that mazal decides a person's physical traits but not whether he is a tzaddik or a rasha, and uses this to explain Iyov's words and the Tanya's definition of a tzaddik as one who has no yetzer hara at all.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara's categories of tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo and the Ra'aya Mehemna's reading of them, then the Gemara in Berachos that the yetzer tov 'judges' the tzaddik, and Rabbah's claim to be a beinoni. He asks how Iyov could say that Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim, when the angel announces at conception whether a person will be rich or poor, wise or foolish, but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha. At length he explains what mazal is: the star and angel over each month, hour and moment of birth, and the place of birth, from which a person's physical traits flow down. Since Rabbah never sinned, a beinoni must be one who never sins; the Rosh Hashanah 'tzaddik' is a borrowed name. A true tzaddik has no yetzer hara, like Dovid HaMelech. Some are born so, and of these rare individuals Iyov spoke.

en: The angel at conception announces a person's physical lot (rich or poor, wise or foolish, strong or weak) but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha, since that is left to his free choice.
Mazal is the star and its angel over the month, hour and moment of birth, and even the country of birth shapes a person; his physical bounty flows down to him through it.
Because Rabbah never sinned and was truthful, his calling himself a beinoni shows that a beinoni is one who never commits a sin.
The 'tzaddik' of the Rosh Hashanah judgment, one with more merits than sins, is only a borrowed name, meaning one who is found right in that judgment.
A true tzaddik has no yetzer hara at all, as Dovid HaMelech said that his heart was 'chalal', empty of it.
Some tzaddikim are born without a yetzer hara and some, like Dovid HaMelech, worked until they lost it; Iyov's words refer to the first kind, who are rare individuals.

title.en: Tzaddik v'tov lo and tzaddik v'ra lo

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's categories of tzaddik v'tov lo, tzaddik v'ra lo and their counterparts. He contrasts the plain reading (a tzaddik who fares well or badly) with the Ra'aya Mehemna's reading, that tzaddik v'ra lo is a tzaddik who has evil within him but rules over it like a master over a dog on a leash.

title.en: Rabbah the beinoni and Iyov's question

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara at the end of Berachos that the yetzer tov is the tzaddik's judge, and Rabbah's statement that he is a beinoni. He then asks how Iyov could say Hashem created tzaddikim and reshaim, when the angel at conception announces a person's physical traits but not whether he will be a tzaddik or a rasha, so as not to compel his choice.

title.en: Mazal: the stars of the months

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every person has a mazal, a star in the heavens in which an angel is clothed. Each month has its own permutation of the Name Havaya and its own mazal, which is why Cheshvan brings withering and Kislev a new light, and a person born in a month carries its traits.

title.en: Hour, place and the meaning of 'mazal'

summary.en: The Mashgiach adds that every hour and moment has its mazal, and that the country of birth also shapes a person, while Eretz Yisroel is above mazal. He explains that 'mazal' means flowing down, like 'nozlim', and that 'gad' also means mazal, and concludes that the angel announces everything by mazal except tzaddik and rasha.

title.en: A beinoni never sins

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what a beinoni is, given that Rabbah never stopped learning and was a man of truth. He goes through the Tanya's definitions of a rasha, including one who could learn and does not, and concludes that since Rabbah had not even bitul Torah, a beinoni must be one who never sins.

title.en: The Rosh Hashanah tzaddik is a borrowed name

summary.en: If a beinoni never sins, the Mashgiach asks, what is a tzaddik, and how does this fit the Gemara in Rosh Hashanah where a tzaddik is one with more merits than sins? He answers that there 'tzaddik' is a borrowed name, like a litigant who wins his din Torah: he is right in that judgment, not a tzaddik in truth.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech's empty heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Dovid HaMelech's words 'v'libi chalal b'kirbi': chalal means empty, so the left chamber of his heart had no yetzer hara, and it also means killed, since he slew it through fasting. A tzaddik is one with no yetzer hara, and such tzaddikim are few, as the Gemara says Hashem planted them in every generation.

title.en: Tzaddikim who are born complete

summary.en: The Mashgiach sets out the Tanya's premise: a tzaddik has no yetzer hara, either from birth or by working until he lost it, while a beinoni has two judges and chooses between them. Tzaddikim born complete come down for the sake of others, and since they have no choice they may remember earlier gilgulim, as the Yismach Moshe remembered being a sheep of Yaakov Avinu.

title.en: Iyov's answer: rare individuals

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Iyov spoke of tzaddikim created complete, and of reshaim born to be wicked, whom Hashem also needs for His plan for creation. Dovid HaMelech instead had to repair Adam's flaw and work until he became a tzaddik; most people are neither, and have the choice to be at least a beinoni.

catalogTitle: שתי נשמות לישראל' טעם שהטומאה נקרא קליפה' ד' קליפות וד' יסודות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's opening teaching that every Jew has two souls, why the side of evil is called sitra achra and klipah, and how the four klipos parallel the four elements.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach begins Tanya chapter one: every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, has two souls. The animal soul gives the biological life a person shares with every creature and comes from the earth; the G-dly soul comes from above and longs to cleave to Hashem. The animal soul comes from the sitra achra, 'the other side', and one cannot stand on both sides of the fence, as the Kotzker's vort about dancing at two weddings shows. It is also called klipah, a shell: it guards the fruit, but it must be broken to reach it, and breaking it is a person's purpose. The Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of the king's seven walls and stories of Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev and Rabbi Aharon of Karlin show the sweetness waiting beyond. He then explains why the animal soul dwells in the blood, and the four klipos parallel to the four elements, illustrated by the layers of a walnut.

en: Every Jew, whether tzaddik or rasha, has two souls: an animal soul from the side of klipah and a G-dly soul that is a part of G-d above.
The animal soul is the life force a person shares with every living creature, and its seat is the blood.
The source of evil is called sitra achra, 'the other side', because one cannot be on both sides of the fence at once.
It is called klipah because, like a shell, it is needed only to guard the fruit, and because it must be broken through to reach the fruit; breaking it is a person's purpose in the world.
There are four klipos, parallel to the four elements that come from the four letters of Hashem's Name; the finest, klipas nogah, lets light through and can be turned to holiness.

title.en: Every Jew has two souls

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter one: every Jew, tzaddik or rasha, has two souls. He explains the animal soul that a person shares with every creature and the G-dly soul from above, mentions a third, intellectual soul that the Tanya does not discuss here, and describes what each of the two souls desires.

title.en: Sitra achra: you cannot dance at two weddings

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the animal soul comes from the sitra achra, Aramaic for 'the other side', and that one cannot stand on both sides of the fence. He brings a vort of the Kotzker about dancing at two weddings, notes that what people say has truth in it, and explains that 'eishes chayil' means either the Torah or a physical wife, but not both together.

title.en: Why evil is called klipah

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives two reasons for the name klipah: a shell only guards the fruit and is thrown away once the fruit is taken, and one must break through the shell to reach the fruit. He ties this to the keruvim and the flaming sword guarding Gan Eden and says breaking the klipah is a person's purpose.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of seven walls

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Ba'al Shem Tov's parable of a king surrounded by seven guarded walls: soldiers stop after the gifts of the first walls, but the prince breaks through all seven to reach his father, who then shows him the walls were only an illusion.

title.en: Wanting the King Himself

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the parable: a person must break the seven walls of the bad middos, and the one who serves Hashem out of love wants only Hashem Himself, as the Ba'al HaTanya would say in his dveikus. He brings the Gemara that the yetzer hara will look to tzaddikim like a mountain and to reshaim like a hair, and Dovid HaMelech's words that Torah is sweeter than honey.

title.en: The poritz's pleasures and a tzaddik's

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, about to light Chanukah candles, asked a man about the poritz's food and bed and concluded that the poritz is well off but he himself is better off, and how Rabbi Aharon of Karlin dismissed a poritz sledding on sugar in midsummer next to his own pleasure in Nishmas on Shabbos. Each person feels the sweetness according to how much klipah he has broken.

title.en: The animal soul dwells in the blood

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that holiness is likened to a nut whose shell must be cracked, then returns to the Tanya's text and its source in Rabbi Chaim Vital. He explains that the animal soul is clothed in the blood, as the passuk says, while the G-dly soul is in the brain, and gives a simple reason why the Torah forbids eating blood.

title.en: Four elements, four klipos, and the walnut

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the four elements come from the four letters of Hashem's Name, and that the four klipos parallel them. He brings Yechezkel's vision of the four barriers before the Kisei HaKavod, explains klipas nogah as a translucent curtain that lets light through and can be turned to holiness, and illustrates the four klipos with the four coverings of a walnut.

catalogTitle: Side 1: Every Jew is an אות & a מצוה Side 2: מתן תורה - The Foundation of Emunah

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach presents Shavuos as a Yovel of return, when every Jew goes back to his own letter and mitzvah in the Torah, and shows that Matan Torah, witnessed by an entire nation, is the foundation of emunah that is relived every year.

abstract.en: In the first talk the Mashgiach approaches Shavuos through the law of Yovel, return. The Eved Ivri who was uprooted from the family of Klal Yisrael goes back at Yovel to his family and his portion in Eretz Yisrael; so too every Jew is one of the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah and is rooted in one of the 613 mitzvos, and Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a small Yovel when he returns to his letter and his mitzvah. He shows this law of return in nature, in the ger, and in Rus and Yisro, calls for heartfelt prayer for Torah, and tells how the Sanzer Rav's son saw Matan Torah anew. In the second talk he reads the pesukim of Va'eschanan and Yisro: an entire nation heard Hashem speak, which no other religion can claim, and this was passed down without a break, so a Jew knows Matan Torah rather than merely believes it. It repeats every Shavuos, and he urges davening and hearing the Torah reading with full kavanah.

en: Shavuos, the fiftieth day after seven weeks of Sefirah, is a miniature Yovel: a day of returning to one's roots.
Every Jew is one letter of the Sefer Torah, corresponding to the 600,000 souls, and belongs exactly in his place in it.
Every Jew is rooted in one particular mitzvah, and the mitzvah of this generation before Moshiach is emunah.
Matan Torah was witnessed by an entire nation who all became prophets, unlike other religions built on one individual's claim.
A tradition witnessed by millions and passed from father to son is irrefutable, so a Jew knows Matan Torah rather than only believing it.
Matan Torah repeats itself every Shavuos, and each Jew receives his portion in Torah for the coming year.

emunah in the generation before Moshiach

title.en: One road to Shavuos: seven weeks to the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach says the Torah, and so Shavuos, is infinite, and he will approach it from one of many roads. He describes the seven weeks of Sefirah leading to the fiftieth day and introduces Yovel, which means return.

title.en: The Eved Ivri returns to his family

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Eved Ivri, permitted to a shifcha, is uprooted from the family of Klal Yisrael; shifcha is mishpacha without the mem. At Yovel he is dragged back to his family and his nachalah, and the Ramban explains Yovel as going back to the roots.

title.en: Shavuos as a miniature Yovel

summary.en: Every Jew has a letter in the Sefer Torah, and one who does not keep it uproots himself. The Mashgiach links the shofar of freedom, the great shofar at Sinai and the shofar of Yovel, calls Shavuos a miniature Yovel, and notes that Parshas Behar on Shemitah and Yovel is read before Shavuos.

title.en: Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: From the counting in Bamidbar, the lots of Eretz Yisrael and the four camps around the Mishkan corresponding to the five Chumashim, the Mashgiach shows that each Jew has his exact place. The ben ha-Mitzri was an extra letter; at hagbahah one tries to see his own letter, and the Shabbos before Shavuos returns each Jew to it.

title.en: Every Jew's own mitzvah; ours is emunah

summary.en: Each Jew is rooted in one of the 613 mitzvos, as Reb Naftali of Ropshitz was bound to the mitzvah of sukkah, and each generation has its mitzvah; the Mashgiach says ours is emunah, which explains today's heresy. The 620 letters of the Aseres Hadibros are the 613 mitzvos plus the seven rabbinic ones, and on Shavuos each Jew binds himself to his letter.

title.en: The law of return: nature, the ger, Rus and Yisro

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows a universal law that everything returns to its source: a thrown stone, water and rivers, as in Koheles, and the neshamah. A ger has a Jewish soul that finds no rest until it returns; therefore on Shavuos we read of Rus who 'returned' and of Yisro, whose names share their letters.

title.en: Praying for Torah; the Sanzer Rav's son sees Matan Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Shavuos is a special time to pray for Torah, recalling tzaddikim whose Ahavah Rabbah lasted hours in tears. Each Shavuos Matan Torah is given again and each Jew gets his portion for the year, a Rosh Hashanah for Torah. He tells how the Sanzer Rav's son, who went to Belz for Shavuos, saw the thunder and lightning of Matan Torah at his father's.

title.en: A people of mesiras nefesh returns to the Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Shavuos is not a commemoration but a reliving of Matan Torah. Jews come from a stock that gave their lives rather than abandon Torah; each should accept the Torah despite hardship, return to his roots and bring others closer. He closes with Shavuos as the day of David HaMelech and a wish for the great Yovel.

title.en: Second talk: Hashem speaks through the Chumash

summary.en: Opening a second talk, the Mashgiach says he will not offer his own derashah: in the Chumash Hashem Himself speaks to us. He asks listeners not to learn Chumash as in cheder but to listen attentively to every word.

title.en: What your eyes saw: a nation of prophets

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'rak hishamer lecha' in Va'eschanan: do not forget what your eyes saw at Chorev. Other religions rest on one charismatic man's claim; at Sinai every Jew became a prophet and heard Hashem face to face, and the pasuk commands passing this to children and grandchildren.

title.en: An irrefutable chain of tradition

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Matan Torah to historical facts no one doubts, since a lie witnessed by multitudes cannot pass down the generations. The Torah was written within forty years while witnesses lived, every Jewish community has the same Sefer Torah, and each generation is a link in the chain.

title.en: The third day at Sinai repeats every year

summary.en: Turning to Parshas Yisro, the Mashgiach reads 'atem re'isem': at the Exodus they saw but were not prophets, while at Sinai they would be. He describes the thunder, lightning and trembling of the third day, and explains that every Yom Tov's event repeats; shanah means repetition, and on Shavuos each Jew receives his Torah for the year.

title.en: Hidden by the body; knowing, not believing

summary.en: Hashem speaks to every Jew on Shavuos, but the body and aveiros insulate us; great tzaddikim showed their talmidim the thunder and lightning. The Mashgiach reads 'ki she'al na': no nation ever heard G-d speak from the fire, and 'atah hor'esa lada'as', as Rav Hirsch stresses, means we know Matan Torah rather than believe it.

title.en: The avodah of Shavuos: hearing and visualizing

summary.en: The Mashgiach says each Yom Tov has its activity, and Shavuos's is hearing the word of Hashem. One should say Ahavah Rabbah with great feeling, visualize standing at Sinai when the Aseres Hadibros are read, and remember Matan Torah, one of the six zechiros. He warns not to stay up all night and then sleep through davening.

title.en: The groom without a ring; a prayer for the shofar of Moshiach

summary.en: With a parable of a groom who pays for everything but the ring, the Mashgiach says the main thing is davening and the Torah reading. He speaks of Klal Yisrael's need for salvation, and closes with the Midrash of Yitzchak's ram: its left horn sounded at Matan Torah and its right horn will be the shofar of Moshiach.
