oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's teaching that the animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, which can be elevated to kedushah, and how all bad middos stem from its four elements: fire, water, air and earth.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's opening: every Jew has an animal soul from the side of kelipah, and the four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name. Three are wholly impure and must be destroyed; the fourth, kelipas nogah, can be transformed, as seen in milah and periah and in the four verbs of the brachah against the wicked. The animal soul of a Jew comes from nogah, so kosher food and natural middos can be raised to kedushah when used for serving Hashem, while a goy's animal soul comes from the three impure kelipos; this is the difference between tzedakah and mere charity. He then goes through the four elements: anger and pride from fire, desire and pleasure from water, frivolity, mockery, boasting and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth, distinguishing sadness from constructive bitterness. He closes with the tree of knowledge of good and evil and the Midrash contrasting olos and shelamim.

en: The four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name; three are wholly impure and must be broken, while the fourth, kelipas nogah, can be turned to kedushah.
The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, while that of a goy comes from the three impure kelipos.
Kosher food eaten for the sake of Heaven, with its strength used for Torah, tefilah and mitzvos, is elevated to kedushah, each according to his level.
All bad middos come from the four elements: anger and pride from fire, desires from water, frivolity, mockery, boasting and idle talk from air, laziness and sadness from earth.
Sadness is not a mitzvah and leads to sin, whereas bitterness over one's state stirs a person to act.
A goy can bring only an olah, which is wholly burned, while a Jew can bring a shelamim whose eating is part of the offering, because a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: Review: the animal soul and the four kelipos

summary.en: After a request to keep up with the series on tape, the Mashgiach reviews the Tanya's words that every Jew has an animal soul from kelipah, from which all bad middos come, and that the four kelipos are the dross of the four letters of Hashem's Name, from which the four elements of all creation come.

title.en: Three impure kelipos and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the first three kelipos are wholly impure and must be cut away, like the layers removed at milah, while nogah, like periah, is turned upward, and he finds the same four in the verbs of the brachah against the wicked in Nusach Ari. Forbidden food comes from the three, kosher food from nogah, and nogah is translucent; the four kelipos appear in Yechezkel's vision in chapter one.

title.en: A Jew's animal soul and elevating food

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the animal soul is the life force a person shares with all creatures, distinct from the breath of life Hashem blew into Adam. A Jew's animal soul comes from nogah and a goy's from the three impure kelipos, and with the example of a piece of kosher chicken he shows how the same food is dragged down or raised to kedushah depending on how it is eaten and used.

title.en: Natural middos: tzedakah versus charity

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that a person's natural middos, such as a love of giving, come from the animal soul; used for Heaven they are raised from nogah, used for evil they fall to the sitra achra. He distinguishes a Jew's tzedakah from a goy's charity, which is the animal kindness every creature has and is done for oneself, citing the Gemara that the kindness of the nations is a sin.

title.en: Fire: the source of anger and pride

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that all bad middos come from the four elements, beginning with anger and pride from fire. Every object holds all four elements, as burning wood shows, which he compares to modern science's matter and energy. Fire rises because its root is in the moon, which he says is why bedikas chametz is done at night.

title.en: Water and air: desire, frivolity, mockery

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that desire and pleasure come from water, the first element, linked to chesed and to the first of the seven voices; all pleasure and all life involve water, and water draws and attracts. From air come frivolity and mockery: wild music that releases a person from all restraint, and jokes, whose humor lies in their distance from reality.

title.en: Boasting, idle talk, and earth: sadness versus bitterness

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes boasting and idle talk as hollow air, with the picture of an honoree at a charity banquet. From earth come laziness and sadness, which leave a person lying idle; he contrasts sadness with bitterness that drives a person to act, brings a saying of Reb Aharon of Karlin, and shows from the Gemara and Rashi that sadness is never a mitzvah.

title.en: Good middos, the tree of knowledge, olah and shelamim

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that even a Jew's inborn good middos, like mercy and kindness, come from the body and so from kelipas nogah, which holds good, as the secret of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. He brings the Midrash on 'awake, north, and come, south': the nations bring olos slaughtered in the north, Jews bring shelamim that are eaten, because only a Jew can eat for the sake of Heaven, apart from the few chasidei umos haolam who keep the seven mitzvos as the Rambam rules.

catalogTitle: שלש קליפות הטמאות אין להם תיקון עד ביאת המשיח. גוף ישראל מקליפת נוגה' ושל גוים משלש קליפות הטמאות - לפיכך חסד לאומים חטאת.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Tanya chapter one: the Jewish animal soul comes from klipas nogah, which can be elevated, while the nations' souls come from the three impure klipos, which have no tikkun until Moshiach, and therefore even the kindness of the nations is called a sin.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the rule that the three impure klipos cannot be elevated until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, the permitted pleasures, can. He asks how a forbidden mixture can then be nullified in sixty, and answers that such nullification is a glimmer of the days of Moshiach, as at the Exodus. He then reads the Tanya: even a Jew's animal soul is from nogah, while the nations' souls are from the impure klipos, so all the good they do is for themselves, even their mercy and charity. A Jew's mercy can become a mitzvah, shown in a story of a man who gave charity first from pity and then for the mitzvah. Through Yaakov's weeping at meeting Rachel, the Sukkah parable and the Maggid of Mezritch, he shows that a Jew's love and service are at root for Hashem. He closes with the Gemara on 'the kindness of nations is a sin' and explains chatas and zechus.

en: The three impure klipos have no tikkun until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, the permitted pleasures, can be elevated to holiness.
A Jew's animal soul comes from klipas nogah, while the vitalizing soul of the nations comes from the three impure klipos.
All the good the nations do, even out of mercy and charity, they do for themselves and not for Hashem.
A Jew's mercy, which comes from nogah, can be turned into the mitzvah of tzedakah and holiness.
Yaakov's love for Rachel was a love from holiness, not a physical self-love, which is why seven years seemed to him like a few days.
Every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, so even his service not for its own sake contains something for Hashem's sake.
The word chatas is one of the names of the impure side, while zechus comes from 'zach', pure: the root of all evil is self-interest and the root of all good is acting not for oneself.

candidateTopics: klipas nogah and the three impure klipos
marriage as a bond of souls

title.en: Impure klipos versus klipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the three impure klipos, the forbidden pleasures, cannot be elevated until Moshiach, while klipas nogah, permitted Jewish pleasure, can. He asks how a forbidden thing can then be nullified in sixty, and answers that such nullification is a glimmer of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The Exodus, the chazir and redemption

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that at the Exodus even the impure klipos were nullified, and brings the Ohr HaChaim on why the pig is called chazir, that it will one day return. He explains that redemption cannot be taken on one's own but comes from Hashem's remembering, and contrasts the Jewish animal soul from nogah with the gentile soul from the impure klipos, which can do nothing for Hashem.

title.en: The Tanya: the nations do good for themselves

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that even the Jewish animal soul is from nogah while the nations' souls are from the three impure klipos with no good at all, so all the good they do is for themselves. Even their mercy is the animal trait shared by all creatures, and they give charity so that they can enjoy their own supper.

title.en: Mercy that becomes a mitzvah; 'the kindness of nations is a sin'

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a man who took in a hungry poor man, gave him everything out of pity, and then added a large sum for the mitzvah of tzedakah. He explains that a Jew's mercy, from nogah, can become a mitzvah, while the nations' kindness is called a sin because they do it to boast that they are good.

title.en: Why Yaakov wept when he kissed Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why Yaakov wept when he kissed Rachel, brings the Midrash that people suspected him and Rashi that he saw she would not be buried with him. Through the Gemara that kiddushin is learned from Avraham's purchase of the Machpelah field, he explains that a Jewish marriage is a bond of the soul that continues after death, so the separation in burial pained Yaakov.

title.en: Self-love versus Yaakov's love for Rachel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that physical love is really love of oneself, like loving chicken, which one eats. Yaakov loved Rachel because she was a tzaddekes and part of his soul, and the pain over burial shows it was not physical love. He then asks how seven years could seem like a few days to one who loved so strongly.

title.en: The parable of building a Sukkah

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers with a parable: a Jew who builds his Sukkah in the rain with joy does so because the building itself is for Hashem and part of the mitzvah, so long hours feel like minutes. Yaakov's work for Rachel was like building a Sukkah, a love from holiness, so the years seemed like a few days.

title.en: Hidden love, lishmah and the Maggid of Mezritch

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has a hidden love for Hashem, brings a saying of Reb Aharon of Karlin, and says that even a Jew's service not for its own sake holds something for Hashem's sake. He tells how the Maggid of Mezritch, his family starving, sighed, heard that he had lost his world to come, and then learned with great joy now that he could serve purely for Hashem.

title.en: Every Jew is a chassid; the gentile's good

summary.en: The Mashgiach says every Jew at root is a chassid who would do a mitzvah even without reward, and this inner light brings him back. A gentile's good deeds, even when he thinks they are for Heaven, come from the three impure klipos, except for a spark of holiness that can lead to conversion; by contrast, even a Jew's ordinary dealings can be for a mitzvah.

title.en: Chatas and zechus; all will become good

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara on 'the kindness of nations is a sin': their charity adds to their merit and delays the redemption, as with the Emori. He explains that chatas is a name of the impure side, while zechus comes from zach, pure: the root of evil is self-interest and the root of good is acting not for oneself. He closes that in the time of Moshiach even the three impure klipos will become good.

catalogTitle: הנשמות חלק אלקי ממעל ממש' 'בנים' אתם לה' אלוקיכם; קשיא: איך יש מדריגות בנשמות אם כלם אלקות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why every Jewish soul is 'truly a part of G-d above' and a child of Hashem drawn from His wisdom, and then takes up the question of how there can be levels among souls, answering with the image of one body from head to heel that runs through the generations down to our own, the heel before Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach learns the opening of Tanya chapter two: the second soul of a Jew is truly a part of G-d. From the verse that Hashem breathed into Adam the breath of life, and the saying that one who breathes, breathes from within himself, he shows that this breath carries Hashem's innermost being, which is why the shofar is blown with a cry beyond words. The daily blessing 'You breathed it into me' shows this holds for every Jew. The soul rose in Hashem's thought, and Jews are called His children: as a child is drawn from the father's brain, every soul is drawn from Hashem's wisdom. Since Hashem is Himself the knowledge, as the Rambam writes, the human brain, made for this world, cannot grasp it; the soul and ruach hakodesh can, and the rest is received and believed. He then asks how levels among souls are possible, and explains that one body has a head and a heel, and so do the world and the generations, down to our own heel generation, where truth is lacking.

en: The verse that Hashem 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' shows that the soul comes from Hashem's innermost being, since one who breathes breathes from within himself.
The daily blessing 'You breathed it into me' shows that this breath of Hashem is in every Jew, not only in Adam.
Jews are called children of Hashem because, as a child is drawn from the father's brain, every Jewish soul is drawn from Hashem's thought and wisdom.
The human brain was created to understand this world, so it cannot grasp Hashem, who is Himself the knowledge and the knower; this is grasped only by the soul.
The Mashgiach asks how there can be greater and lesser souls if all of them come from Hashem's wisdom, just as all of a man's children are equally his children.
Like the limbs of one body from head to heel, there are levels in the world and in the generations, and our generation is the heel before Moshiach, which hardly feels.

candidateTopics: the soul as a part of G-d
breath of life and the shofar

title.en: Breathed from within: the soul and the shofar

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens Tanya chapter two, that the second soul of a Jew is truly a part of G-d, and explains the verse of Hashem breathing the breath of life into Adam: one who breathes, breathes from within, so the soul carries Hashem's innermost being. He connects this to Rosh Hashanah, when this breath is blown back through the shofar with a cry beyond words.

title.en: Every Jew says 'You breathed it into me'

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how we know the breath of Hashem is in every Jew and not only in Adam, and answers from the daily blessing instituted by the Men of the Great Assembly, 'You breathed it into me'. He shows that breath is the inner life of a person, as the signs of life in the Shulchan Aruch, a feather or a cold mirror at the nose, test for breath.

title.en: Risen in thought: Jews as Hashem's children

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Chazal's words that Israel rose in Hashem's thought and the verses calling Jews Hashem's children. A child is drawn from the father's brain, and so every Jewish soul is drawn from Hashem's thought and wisdom.

title.en: He is the knowledge and the knower

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that Hashem is the knowledge and the knower: a person's knowledge comes from outside and is separate from him, while Hashem's knowledge is Himself. Following the Tanya, he says this cannot be grasped by a human mind, as the verse asks whether one can find out G-d.

title.en: The brain was made for this world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the brain, like the hands, feet and lungs, is a part of the body made for this world, and it interprets what the five senses take in, as with the eye that sees upside down. Just as a painting cannot be heard however strong the ears, the brain cannot grasp G-dliness.

title.en: The soul perceives what the mind cannot

summary.en: The Mashgiach says there is a sense that perceives G-dliness: a Jew with ruach hakodesh perceives through his soul, not his mind, since sins have not cut him off from it. The mind grasps Hashem's oneness with His wisdom only through emunah; it was received from those with ruach hakodesh that every soul comes from Hashem's wisdom, like a child from the father's brain, and one who does not understand must believe.

title.en: The question: how can souls differ?

summary.en: The Mashgiach raises the Tanya's question: there are countless levels of souls, from the Avos and Moshe Rabbeinu down to our generations. If greater souls came from wisdom and lesser ones from lower powers it would be understood, but if all come from wisdom and are equally children, why are they not equal? He announces that he will step aside to explain another matter in order to reach the answer.

title.en: From head to heel: body, world and generations

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that one person's body has levels, from the head with its wisdom down to the heel, and the world too has limbs: Yerushalayim is its heart. So too the generations, from those that are the head down to the heels, and within each generation. He shows that the heel hardly feels a needle because it is farthest from the head, the source of all feeling.

title.en: The heel before Moshiach and the descent after the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara in Sotah that the last generation before Moshiach is called its heels, and says the Arizal already headed the heel souls while the Ba'al HaTanya called his generations the heels of Moshiach. He shows the same descent at the beginning of Klal Yisrael: the Avos, then the tribes, then the seventy souls who went down to Egypt, and with Yaakov Avinu's passing the heels began.

title.en: Our generation: the heel, where truth is missing

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that with Moshe Rabbeinu and the generation of Matan Torah the order began again from the heads, and descended down to our generation, the very bottom of the heel, which feels nothing and stands in darkness. He brings the Gemara that chutzpah grows before Moshiach and truth is missing, and shows it in Krias Shema, whose last word corresponds to the lowest limb and where the word emes is not written in the passage.

catalogTitle: The קדושה of שיר השירים as the Theme of שבועות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael, the moment the holiness of Shir HaShirim came down to the world, and that the seven weeks of Sefirah are the kallah's preparation through purifying the seven middos.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with this week's mitzvah of rebuke and explains, with the example of an inoculation, why anger shows the rebuke has worked. Turning to Sefirah, he shows that the tenth of the ten utterances of creation is the creation of chassan and kallah, the culmination of the world. Shlomo HaMelech, whose wisdom could only be conveyed through layers of parables, wrote Shir HaShirim as the parable of the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael. Shabbos is the kallah, and the tenth and highest holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, corresponds to that union, which is why Shir HaShirim is the holy of holies of Tanach. At Matan Torah this holiness came down into the physical world, so Shavuos is the wedding and the Luchos are the kiddushin. The seven weeks of Sefirah are the kallah's days of purification: refining chesed, gevurah, tiferes, netzach and hod, each embodied by a tzaddik. He closes with the Rambam's laws of holiness and purity in the Sefirah sedros and a story of the Bluzhever Rebbe whose heart raced before Shavuos.

en: When the one being rebuked becomes angry, it shows the rebuke has stirred him, like the reaction that shows an inoculation is working, so the mitzvah has been fulfilled.
The tenth utterance of creation is the creation of chassan and kallah, the culmination of the world, which is why the wedding blessing uses the word 'bara'.
Shir HaShirim is Shlomo HaMelech's parable for the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, which the human mind cannot grasp directly.
The tenth and highest holiness, the Kodesh HaKodashim, corresponds to the tenth utterance, the union of chassan and kallah, and Shir HaShirim is the Kodesh HaKodashim of Tanach.
Shavuos is the wedding of Hashem with Knesses Yisrael; the Luchos are the kiddushin, and therefore they rest in the Kodesh HaKodashim.
The seven weeks of Sefirah are like the kallah's seven days of purity, given to purify the seven middos before coming to the chuppah.

candidateTopics: Shavuos as the wedding of Hashem and Klal Yisrael
Shir HaShirim as holy of holies

title.en: Rebuke and the sign that it worked

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara's dispute on how far one must rebuke, asks how it knows rebuke continues until the other gets angry, and answers with an inoculation: the angry reaction shows the rebuke is working and the mitzvah is done.

title.en: The tenth utterance: chassan and kallah

summary.en: Turning to Sefirah as preparation for Matan Torah, the Mashgiach discusses the ten utterances of creation and shows that the tenth, the creation of chassan and kallah, is the culmination of creation; he then introduces Shlomo HaMelech and his parables.

title.en: Shlomo HaMelech's three thousand parables

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks what is special about Shlomo's parables, and explains in the name of the Ba'al HaTanya that his thought was so deep that he had to lower it through three thousand parables, each explaining the one above, before people began to grasp it.

title.en: Shir HaShirim and the menuchah of Shabbos

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Shir HaShirim as speaking of chassan and kallah, tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov and a boy singing it with fervor, and explains from Rashi that what was created on Shabbos is menuchah, the settledness of a married woman.

title.en: Shir HaShirim as the Kodesh HaKodashim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shir HaShirim is the parable for the union of Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, that Shabbos is the kallah, and that the tenth of the ten holinesses, the Kodesh HaKodashim with its keruvim, corresponds to that union; therefore Rabbi Akiva calls Shir HaShirim holy of holies.

title.en: Matan Torah as the wedding

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that at Matan Torah the holiness of Shir HaShirim came down into the physical world; Matan Torah was like a chuppah, wedding customs mirror it, Shavuos is the day of the nesuin, and the Luchos are the kiddushin kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim.

title.en: Sefirah: purifying the middos

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Sefirah to the kallah's seven days of purity, asks why the Torah says so little about middos, and answers that good middos are the prerequisite for Torah; Sefer Bereishis teaches middos through the Avos, and in these weeks one must purify seven middos.

title.en: Chesed, gevurah and Yishmael

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains chesed as love, used for good or for indulgence, with Avraham as its tzaddik; gevurah as holding back, embodied by Yitzchak; and Yishmael as the refuse of Avraham's chesed, like the side effects of a medicine.

title.en: Tiferes, netzach, hod and their blends

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Esav as the klipah of gevurah and Yaakov as the blend called tiferes, like harmony in color and music; from Pasach Eliyahu he explains netzach and hod as the two legs, standing by fighting or by yielding; and with a mother holding her child he shows gevurah within chesed.

title.en: Kedushah and taharah in the Sefirah sedros

summary.en: The Mashgiach points out that all the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah are found in the sedros read during Sefirah, from Shemini to Kedoshim, because these are days of holiness and purity before the chuppah.

title.en: The Bluzhever Rebbe's racing heart

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how a doctor found the Bluzhever Rebbe's heart beating abnormally shortly before Shavuos, and the Rebbe answered that he was about to receive the Torah; he closes that Shavuos must not come unprepared, since then the Torah of the whole year is given anew.

catalogTitle: תשובה: בכל דור יש קומה שלימה והמדריגות בנשמות נמשכות מענין השתלשלות העולמות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 2, that every generation and all souls together form one complete body like Adam haRishon's, and that the differences between souls come only from the changes a soul undergoes on its way down, not from its essence.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the generations from Moshe Rabbeinu to the heels of Moshiach form one shiur komah, and adds that each single generation does too. He brings Chazal that Adam haRishon was the challah of the world, explains why challah is baked for Shabbos, and how every person was once a part of Adam's body: head, hands, feet, even nails and hair, each with its own kind of avodah. Turning to the Tanya, he asks how souls can differ in rank if each is truly a part of G-d. His answer is hishtalshelus: like water turning to steam or ice, or a drop from the father's brain that becomes nails over nine months, the soul stays the same essence and only its outer state changes. In the future all will be equal, like dancers in a circle. He ends with the Tanya's Aramaic word for the lowest levels and with the lowest generation before Moshiach.

en: Not only all the generations together, but every single generation forms a complete shiur komah, with souls of the head, the hands and down to the heels.
Every person was once a part of Adam haRishon's body, and the part he came from shapes the kind of avodah he is drawn to: Torah, tefillah, chesed or mitzvos.
Since every soul is truly a part of G-d, the differences between souls cannot come from their essence; they come from the changes of the descent.
Like water that becomes steam or ice, or a drop from the father's brain that becomes nails, the soul remains the same substance through all its changes.
In the future the differences will vanish: like a circle dance, where no one is at the head, even the lowest souls will be raised to the level of the highest.
Changes that are only accidental cannot last; what has been changed must in the end return to its first state.

candidateTopics: Adam haRishon as the shiur komah of all souls
equality of souls in the future

title.en: Adam haRishon as the challah of the world

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that the generations from Moshe Rabbeinu to the heels of Moshiach form one body, and adds that each generation does too. He brings that Adam haRishon was the challah of the world, kneaded off from the earth like a piece of dough, and explains why baking challah for Shabbos on Erev Shabbos rectifies Chavah's sin and brings blessing to the whole week.

title.en: Every soul was a limb of Adam haRishon

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a thought he heard about the shitin under the mizbeach, from whose place Adam was taken, and explains that all souls were contained in Adam's body. Those from the head are drawn to Torah, others to tefillah, the hands to chesed, the feet to mitzvos, and those from the nails and hair are the ones who get cut off.

title.en: Cut-off nails, each one's task, and the fern

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ba'al Shem Tov grieved over the Frankists and was told from Heaven that they were cut-off parts. He explains that each person's pull to a particular avodah reflects where he stood in Adam's body, brings the Tanya on tzedakah in the heels of Moshiach, and compares the generations to a fern whose every leaf repeats the shape of the whole.

title.en: The Tanya's levels of souls and the question

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on the many levels of souls, from Moshe Rabbeinu down to the souls of the heels of Moshiach, and within every generation, and within nefesh itself. He then asks: if every soul is truly a part of G-d, how can one be greater and another smaller?

title.en: Hishtalshelus: water, steam and ice

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that the levels come from the soul's descent. He uses the mashal of water: heat (chesed, spreading) turns it to steam and vapor, cold (din, contraction) turns it to ice, yet it is the same substance. He then begins the Tanya's mashal of the drop from the father's brain that changes as it goes down.

title.en: The drop that becomes nails in nine months

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the halachic sign that a child whose hair and nails are complete was carried nine months, and explains it: the brain forms first, and only after nine months of change does the same drop become nails and hair. So too the souls: the lowest are the same drop, only changed.

title.en: Same essence, and the circle dance of the future

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that lower souls are not of a lower root; the surroundings they descended into changed them, while within they are all equal. He brings that in the future Hashem will make a circle dance for the tzaddikim, where no one sits at the head, and the navi's words comparing Yisrael to the children of Kush: the difference is only in the skin.

title.en: Head and heel in place and time

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the same structure in place and time: Eretz Yisrael is the head of the world, as Rosh Hashanah is the head of the year, Nissan begins the months and Adar is the heel, and some lands outside Eretz Yisrael are the heel. He then rereads the Tanya's words on the levels of souls.

title.en: The Aramaic word and the generation of the heel

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when Yaakov lifted his feet he raised the souls of the feet, the lowest, of today's generation. He notes that the Tanya, written in loshon hakodesh, suddenly uses an Aramaic word for the end of all levels, because Targum is a low level. He concludes that even the nails come from the same drop, that accidental changes must return to the first state, and that on the Erev Shabbos before Moshiach some Jews are cut off while others come to repair.

catalogTitle: ביאור האחדות בנשמות אפ' במדריגתם' יעקב חבל נחלתו - כל יהודי יש לו כח השפעה על כל ישראל.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter two, the Mashgiach explains that all Jewish souls, from the greatest tzaddik to the simplest Jew, form one rope, 'Yaakov chevel nachalaso', so that each one draws from and affects all the others.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's words that the souls of the simple folk descend from the same root in Chochmah as the souls of all Israel, through the chain of the four worlds. He explains tzimtzum as the din that lets chesed be received, the meaning of Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, and compares the descent to water turning into ice. The soul of a simple Jew is of the same essence as a great tzaddik's, only more contracted, which is why even a sinner will give his life for Hashem. Using 'Yaakov chevel nachalaso' he describes the Jewish people as one rope from head to heel, and brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef: a great man's fall and a simple Jew's weakening in emunah affect each other. He ends with how the simple Jew cleaves to Hashem through the talmid chacham, receiving face to face or from behind, and why the receiver must humble himself before the giver.

en: Tzimtzum is the measure of din that makes it possible to receive Hashem's chesed, like limiting the flow of milk so a baby can drink.
The souls of simple Jews are of the same essence as those of the greatest tzaddikim; they only underwent more tzimtzum on the way down.
Because every soul stays bound to its root in Chochmah, even the greatest sinner is ready for mesirus nefesh when it comes to denying Hashem.
The Jewish people is one rope, 'Yaakov chevel nachalaso', from Yisrael at the head to Yaakov at the heel; it is not made of separate pieces.
Each Jew is asked for service according to his level, and a failing at one level affects Jews at other levels in both directions.
The simple Jew cleaves to Hashem through the talmid chacham, and influence flows down a ladder of leaders to the tzaddik of the generation.
A receiver must humble himself before the giver to receive, as a cup must be held lower than the jug.

candidateTopics: mutual responsibility between tzaddik and simple Jew
Shabbos as the source of blessing
bittul of the receiver to the giver

title.en: Tzimtzum as din that allows chesed

summary.en: After brief opening words, the Mashgiach reads the Tanya's passage on the souls of the simple folk descending through the four worlds, links the four worlds to the four letters of Hashem's Name, and explains tzimtzum as din that makes chesed receivable, with the mashal of a baby's bottle.

title.en: The four worlds from Atzilus to Asiyah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the word Atzilus from 'atzilei bnei Yisroel' as nearness to the King, then describes Beriah as the start of creation and seat of the Kisei HaKavod, Yetzirah as taking form, and Asiyah as the lowest world.

title.en: Simple souls of the same essence

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach explains that the souls of amei ha'aretz are not lesser in essence but only more contracted, like water that becomes ice, and describes the future circle dance of the tzaddikim and the power of a gathered multitude.

title.en: The chain of worlds and the root in Chochmah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains hishtalshelus as a chain of linked rings, and reads that even the lowest souls remain bound to their root in Chochmah, which is why even a sinner will give his life rather than deny Hashem; the simple souls draw their life from the souls of the tzaddikim.

title.en: Yaakov chevel nachalaso: one rope

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the passuk 'Yaakov chevel nachalaso': Yisrael contains 'li rosh', Yaakov contains 'ekev', so Yaakov spans every level from head to heel, beginning with the yud, the point from which everything starts; all Jews are one rope, not separate pieces.

title.en: One body, and service by each level

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares Klal Yisrael to one body, where pain in the heel is felt in the head, introduces the Toldos Yaakov Yosef's reading of 'Hoshia Hashem ki gamar chasid', and explains that emunah is the base level of every Jew and that each is asked for service according to his level.

title.en: The tzaddik and the simple Jew affect each other

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when great Jews slip, the simplest fall further, and that a simple Jew's sins harm the tzaddik; he brings the Toldos Yaakov Yosef's reading of the passuk and the dream that it can be read the other way, and concludes that both are true.

title.en: Constant dveikus and the Rebbe Reb Elimelech

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's mashal of the nails drawing from the brain, and the Gemara on cleaving to talmidei chachamim; tzaddikim cleave to Hashem constantly while a simple Jew reaches it in high moments. He tells how the Rebbe Reb Elimelech woke when Reb Zusha covered the mezuzah.

title.en: Through the talmid chacham, face to face

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the simple Jew cleaves to Hashem through an intermediary, the talmid chacham, up a ladder of leaders to the tzaddik of the generation; he raises the question of those who oppose talmidei chachamim and introduces two kinds of influence, face to face and from behind.

title.en: Shabbos blesses the week; bowing to receive

summary.en: Through the Zohar that all blessings of the week come from Shabbos, the Mashgiach explains that the talmid chacham sustains the am ha'aretz who supports him, that even an opponent draws from him from behind, and that a receiver must humble himself before the giver, like a cup held below the jug.

catalogTitle: ע"י הכנעה לתלמידי חכמים זוכים ליניקה משפע עליונה' והשפעה לפושעים ומורדים היא ע"י בחינת אחוריים.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains from Tanya chapter two that every Jew draws his life through bittul to the talmidei chachamim, while those who quarrel with them draw it only 'from behind', and that the parents' holiness shapes the body and its mazal but never the soul itself.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter two: since all souls form one chain reaching up to Chochmah Ila'ah, even the simplest Jew must cleave to the talmid chacham, and through him to the Shechinah. He describes the order of the generation, like the banners in the desert, up to the tzaddik hador, revealed or hidden. Hachnaah is a foundation; a cup must be lower than the pitcher to receive. From Pharaoh he learns, with the Sfas Emes, that the sin is not wanting to be humble. Those who quarrel with talmidei chachamim still receive 'from behind', and their envy itself betrays a hidden bittul. He then explains why the parents' sanctity matters: they give the body, its mazal and nature, while Hashem gives the soul. Examples from Avraham, Dovid, Reb Shimon Yaroslaver and the influence of one's country show that a coarse body can be overcome, and that later generations have more refined bodies but smaller souls.

en: Because all souls are linked in one chain, even the lowest must be bound to the talmid chacham, who is bound to the Shechinah.
Hachnaah, submitting to those greater than oneself, is the channel through which a person receives, as a cup must stand lower than what is poured into it.
Those who quarrel with talmidei chachamim still draw from them, but only 'from behind', without a face-to-face bond.
The parents give the body, its nature and its mazal; Hashem gives the soul, which does not depend on them.
A coarse body makes avodas Hashem harder but can be broken through, and Heaven judges a person by what can be expected of him.
Being born in a given country brings something of that country's nature onto a Jew's body, which he can refine.

title.en: Cleaving to the talmid chacham

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on cleaving to talmidei chachamim and explains that since all souls are one chain, the simple Jew is bound to Hashem through the talmid chacham. He describes the order of the generation, like the banners in the desert, up to the tzaddik hador, revealed or hidden.

title.en: Hachnaah as the root of receiving

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who does not respect tzaddikim tears himself from his source, and tells of a Rebbe whose concern, when a man did not stand for him, was for the man. He calls hachnaah a foundation, compares it to a cup below a pitcher, and learns from Pharaoh, with the Sfas Emes, that the real failing is not even wanting to be humble.

title.en: Receiving 'from behind'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's words that rebels and quarrelers draw from the talmidei chachamim 'from behind', within the order of giver and receiver that sustains all creation. Their hatred, he says, comes from envy: deep down they know the ehrlicher Jew is better, and that pain is itself a kind of hachnaah.

title.en: Why the parents' sanctity matters

summary.en: The Mashgiach restates the Tanya's principle that the smallest soul is bound to Hashem like the greatest, then asks why the Zohar Chadash makes a child's greatness depend on the parents' thoughts. He answers with the Gemara's three partners: the parents give the body, Hashem gives the soul.

title.en: Mazal: the channel of the body's flow

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains mazal as the star and channel through which bodily influence flows, from the word 'nozel', and with the Gemara of the angel who declares rich or poor, wise or foolish, strong or weak. He tells the Chofetz Chaim's answer about a poor man, and stresses that tzaddik or rasha is not declared.

title.en: A coarse body and a great soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the parents also set the body's nature and refinement, as animals differ in temperament, so a child born in holiness finds avodas Hashem easier. Great tzaddikim had coarse bodies and worked through them, and he brings the Midrash that Avraham Avinu had the greatest soul and the lowest body.

title.en: Shaul and Dovid: measured by one's starting point

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that Shaul was punished for one sin and Dovid not for two, and answers from the mekubalim that Dovid's body came from Lot's daughter, giving him a fierce yetzer hara that he killed. He adds Reb Shimon Yaroslaver's words about his father, and concludes that Heaven measures by what can be expected of a person.

title.en: The mazal of one's country

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Lech lecha me'artzecha' as leaving the mazal of one's land: a soul born outside Eretz Yisroel passes through the channel of that country's sar and its klipah. This explains why Jews from different countries cannot bear each other, and he compares it to entering a shul through the chimney, but says one can refine it, as Avraham did.

title.en: The garment of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on the Zohar Chadash: the soul must be clothed in a garment from the parents, through which it does mitzvos and receives even material bounty, while the soul itself can be lofty even in a child of lowly parents, as with Dovid HaMelech. He ends that our bodies are more refined than earlier generations' though their souls were greater, which explains the sins recorded in Tanach.

catalogTitle: An Explanation of מגילת רות: The redemption of רות, the נשמה of יובל, from the bondage of מואב

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains Megillas Rus as the megillah of Yovel, the return of a lost soul to its roots: Rus, a neshama of Yovel, is drawn out of Moav to Beis Lechem, and even her descendant Menashe is brought back through Hashem's hidden tunnel of teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with Shavuos as a day of Yovel, of returning to one's roots, set against the eved who cuts himself off from the Jewish family and refuses the 'rope' of Shabbos until the shofar of Yovel drags him out. Megillas Rus is the megillah of Yovel; just as Yovel exists in time and in the soul, it has a place, Beis Lechem, the home of David and Moshiach. Naomi, wife of Elimelech, goes to Moav to bring back Rus, a neshama of Yovel. Boaz hints to Rus that Menashe will come from her, and the Mashgiach asks why he would tell her such a painful thing. Through the Gemara's story of Rav Ashi and Menashe, he answers that even Menashe teaches Klal Yisrael how to make hamotzi. He explains Hashem's tunnel for Menashe's teshuvah as yibum, the tikkun of souls, ties it to the neshamos in our bread, and closes with preparing for Shavuos.

en: Shavuos is a day of Yovel: a return of every Jew to his roots and to the Jewish family, which the counting of Klal Yisrael by families prepares.
Yovel exists in time, in the soul and in a place; its place is Beis Lechem, home of David HaMelech and Moshiach, who gathers Jews back to Eretz Yisrael.
Boaz's hint that Menashe would descend from Rus was meant as comfort: even Menashe would teach Klal Yisrael the halacha of hamotzi.
Hashem accepted Menashe's teshuvah through a hidden tunnel because there is a level of Torah higher than the angels can grasp, where every Jew must return.
Yibum is the tikkun of souls, a 'tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod', and it is connected to Moshiach.
Food holds neshamos awaiting their tikkun; eating with washing, a bracha and kavanah elevates them, while careless eating lowers them.

title.en: Shavuos, Yovel and the eved who leaves the family

summary.en: The Mashgiach introduces Rus and Boaz and calls Shavuos a day of Yovel, a return to one's roots. He contrasts the eved who cuts himself off from the Jewish family and refuses the 'rope' of Shabbos, until the shofar of Yovel on Yom Kippur drags him out like a lifeguard.

title.en: Beis Lechem, the place of Yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Megillas Rus the megillah of Yovel and, following the triad of time, place and soul, argues that the place of Yovel is Beis Lechem. David HaMelech and Moshiach, who gathers Jews back, are neshamos of Yovel, and Rachel near Beis Lechem was promised the return.

title.en: Naomi brings Rus out of Moav

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Naomi, wife of Elimelech, had the task of malchus, to bring back lost souls; she went to Moav, the opposite of Yovel, to draw out Rus. He then brings Boaz's words to Rus about dipping her bread in vinegar and the Gemara's reading that it hints at Menashe.

title.en: Menashe's teshuvah and Boaz's painful hint

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of Menashe's wickedness, his captivity in a heated pot, his teshuvah and Hashem digging a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod against the angels. He then asks why Boaz, bound by the prohibition of hurting with words, told Rus about this blemish in her line.

title.en: Menashe appears to Rav Ashi

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Gemara's story of Rav Ashi, who called Menashe 'our friend', and Menashe appearing to him in a dream to ask where one cuts the bread at hamotzi. Rav Ashi taught the answer the next day, and the halacha passed into the Rambam, the Shulchan Aruch and every Jewish table.

title.en: Boaz's comfort and the angels' objection

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that Boaz was comforting Rus: even the rasha from her line would teach Klal Yisrael the halacha of hamotzi. He then asks why Hashem smuggled Menashe in rather than tell the angels they were wrong, and brings the Yerushalmi on who decides the sinner's fate.

title.en: Levels of Torah and the Mishnah's dispute

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that teshuvah answers what the Torah's plain level does not, because there are levels in the soul and in Torah, and every Jew must return to his root. Thus the Mishnah, that Menashe has no share, and the Gemara, that he does, are both true at different levels, and Hashem acts on a level the angels cannot grasp.

title.en: Eretz Yisrael, Moshiach and the first yibum

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the law that a man sentenced abroad who flees to Eretz Yisrael is judged again, because a deeper level of judgment is revealed there; so Moshiach, a neshama of Yovel, brings close every Jew. He then turns to yibum as a tikkun of souls, from Yehuda and Tamar to Boaz and Rus.

title.en: Yibum as a tunnel; neshamos in bread

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls yibum a tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod and ties it to Moshiach. He compares the body's unseen digestion of bread to the hidden tikkun of a neshama in food, and brings the Ba'al Shem Tov that hunger exists because a soul is wrapped in the food.

title.en: Eating with kavanah and Menashe's lesson

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts careless eating with washing, a bracha and kavanah that elevate the neshama in the bread. Baking is the last stage of the bread's tikkun, so the part baked first shows Hashem hurrying its tikkun; this was Menashe's message to Rav Ashi, that Hashem expedites the tikkun of malchus Beis David.

title.en: Preparing for Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to Shavuos as a return to one's roots and notes that the Torah commands preparation, seven weeks of counting, only for Shavuos. He urges using the last week of Sefirah, even after wasted time.

catalogTitle: חלקי הנשמה הם מעשר ספירות. ביאור עשר ספירות.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's statement that each part of the soul is made of ten powers that come down from the ten sefiros, and goes through the ten powers one by one as they show up in a person.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's words that nefesh, ruach and neshamah each contain ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros. He sets out the levels of the soul and the four worlds, and explains that each world, and therefore each part of the soul, is built of ten. A person is a small world, so his ten powers of the soul are an echo of the ten sefiros, not the sefiros themselves. He then defines each power: chochmah as the first flash and binah as the building made from it; chesed as reaching outward and gevurah as pulling back; daas as the bridge that lets the mind govern the middos; tiferes as harmony; netzach and hod as fighting and yielding, the two legs a person stands on; yesod as reproduction; malchus as the receiver that reveals. He closes with the ten makkos, the ten maamaros and the Aseres Hadibros.

en: Each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah is made of ten powers of the soul, because each of the worlds they correspond to is built of ten sefiros.
Man is a small world, so his ten powers of the soul are a lower echo of the ten sefiros with which Hashem created the world, not the holy sefiros themselves.
Chochmah is the first point or flash of an idea, and binah builds it out like a building from bricks; daas is the bridge between the mind and the middos.
Chesed is spreading out of oneself toward another, gevurah is pulling back into oneself, and tiferes is the harmony born from blending them.
Netzach and hod are the two legs that give a person existence: overcoming opposition, and bending so as not to break.
Malchus has nothing of its own; it receives from the other middos and reveals the whole structure, as Hashem's kingship is revealed in creation.
The ten makkos revealed the ten sefiros through which Hashem created the world, and from this came the Aseres Hadibros.

title.en: Ten aspects in each level of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's words that nefesh, ruach and neshamah each contain ten aspects corresponding to the ten sefiros, lists the higher levels of chayah and yechidah, and explains the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah, each made of ten sefiros. He shows how the four letters of Hashem's Name hold ten letters.

title.en: Man as a small world; chochmah and binah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that man is a small replica of creation, so his ten powers of the soul come down from the ten sefiros without being the sefiros themselves. He defines chochmah as the first flash of an idea and binah as building it out like bricks into a building, calls them father and mother, and introduces daas as the link to the middos.

title.en: Chesed and gevurah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains chesed as love that radiates outward and draws another into one's sphere, and gevurah as its opposite: contracting, recoiling and separating, as one recoils from a lion. He notes that the letters of aryeh, lion, equal gevurah in gematria.

title.en: Daas: the bridge between mind and middos

summary.en: Going back to daas, the Mashgiach contrasts a cat that acts on impulse with a person who can think whether now is the time for love or for fear, toward a sin or toward Hashem. Daas is the bridge that lets chochmah and binah control the middos; a brilliant scholar who cannot control his impulses is a ba'al chochmah and binah but not a ba'al daas.

title.en: Tiferes: beauty from harmony

summary.en: The Mashgiach defines tiferes as the power to blend different things into beauty, illustrating with a painting, a sunset, music and rhyming poetry. In Kabbalah tiferes is a blend of chesed and gevurah, which is why Yaakov, the blend of Avraham and Yitzchak, is tiferes; like two voices in harmony, the blend is a new third thing.

title.en: Netzach and hod: fighting and bending

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Pasach Eliyahu, which maps the sefiros onto the human form, with netzach and hod as the two legs on which a person stands. Netzach gives existence by overcoming, hod by bending, as the grass survives a hurricane that breaks the tree; a tiger has only netzach, while a person has both and needs daas to know which to use.

title.en: Yesod and malchus

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains yesod as the power to reproduce, notes that his explanations are only a drop in the sea but a handle to build on, and explains malchus as a vessel that has nothing of its own, like the moon and like Shabbos, and that reveals Hashem's kingship, as a king and as Dovid Hamelech.

title.en: Ten makkos, ten maamaros, ten dibros

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the ten makkos each revealed one of the ten sefiros of creation, with makkas bechoros corresponding to keser, the very beginning. Once the ten maamaros were revealed, the Jews accepted Hashem's kingship and received the Aseres Hadibros, and he speaks of receiving them again when they are read this Shabbos.

catalogTitle: מוחין נקראים אמות' מדות נקראים כפולות; ביאור חב"ד.

oneLiner.en: Learning Tanya chapter 3, the Mashgiach explains why the intellect is called the 'mothers' and the middos the 'doubles', and builds from the yud of Hashem's Name to the hidden point in every Jew that sin never reaches, and to chochmah as the spark from nothing that binah develops.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens chapter 3 of Tanya: the mochin are called 'mothers' because they are only good, while the middos are 'doubles' because each can serve good or bad. Every level of the soul contains ten powers, like the four letters of Hashem's Name and the four worlds. The tip of the yud is the highest point, the inner point of a Jew that sin does not touch; this is why a sinner receives thirty-nine lashes and not forty, why there are thirty-nine melachos, and what the Kodesh HaKodashim, Yom Kippur, Purim and Parshas Shekalim express, including the haftorah about Yehoash. Returning to the text, he shows the middos as the children of chochmah, binah and daas, mapped onto the days of Creation, and explains chochmah as the first flash of an idea, a 'koach mah' out of nothing, and binah as the building made from it, from which love and fear of Hashem are born.

en: The three mochin are called 'mothers' because at root they are only good; the seven middos are called 'doubles' because each one can be used for good or for bad.
Every part of the soul, nefesh, ruach and neshamah and above, contains all ten powers from chochmah to malchus, parallel to the four letters of Hashem's Name and the four worlds.
The tip of the yud is the innermost point of a Jew, the Kodesh HaKodashim within him, which sin never reaches; therefore a sinner receives thirty-nine lashes rather than forty.
Yom Kippur and Purim reveal this untouched point; Parshas Shekalim, the 'yud' of the four parshiyos, carries the point of Purim.
The middos are the children of chochmah, binah and daas, just as the seven days of Creation, beginning with chesed, came from the higher powers.
Chochmah is the first point or flash of an idea, a 'koach mah' that comes from nothing; binah is the power that develops it into a full building.
When chochmah and binah contemplate the greatness of Hashem, filling and surrounding all worlds, they give birth to love and fear of Hashem.

title.en: Mochin are 'mothers', middos are 'doubles'

summary.en: Continuing chapter 3, the Mashgiach reviews the ten sefiros and explains that the middos, like chesed, can be good or bad, while the mochin are at root only good; even daas of kelipah draws from a good root. That is why the mochin are 'mothers' and the middos 'doubles'.

title.en: Ten powers in every level; a word on Kabbalah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that each of nefesh, ruach and neshamah contains ten powers, and ties the levels of the soul to the four letters of Hashem's Name and the four worlds. He remarks that Chassidus is built on Kabbalah but in the way of avodah, and that learning Kabbalah alone is a danger.

title.en: The tip of the yud: thirty-nine, not forty

summary.en: The four letters of Hashem's Name, each containing ten, make forty, but the tip of the yud is a point sin cannot reach. The Mashgiach uses this to explain why a sinner gets thirty-nine lashes, why there are thirty-nine melachos tied to Adam HaRishon's curses, and why Yom Kippur, the Kohen Gadol's entry into the Kodesh HaKodashim, and Purim, which is even higher, reveal that point.

title.en: Parshas Shekalim and the haftorah of Yehoash

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that Parshas Shekalim is the 'yud' of the four parshiyos and holds the point of Purim and the atonement of Yom Kippur. He tells how Yehoash was hidden in the Kodesh HaKodashim and later sinned and killed Zechariah, and answers why his story is read: the Kodesh HaKodashim is not reached by sin, which is why there are thirty-nine lashes and not forty.

title.en: Three mothers, seven days of building

summary.en: Back in the text, the ten powers divide into three mothers, chochmah, binah and daas, and seven doubles, the seven days of building. The Mashgiach explains that daas directs the middos, unlike in an animal or a child, and shows the middos as the children of chabad, tracing chesed and gevurah in the first two days of Creation.

title.en: Chochmah as the point, binah as the building

summary.en: After a remark that the Ba'al HaTanya has laid the foundations, the Mashgiach explains chochmah as the first point of thought and binah as the building developed from it, matched to the yud and heh of Hashem's Name. He describes the sudden flash of an idea, in Torah learning and in science, as nearly prophecy, and stresses that Tanya speaks of the power to have it.

title.en: Koach mah, and the birth of love and fear

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's words that chochmah is 'koach mah', a power from nothing, compares it to Moshe's humility, and explains binah as developing that point. Chochmah and binah are father and mother, and when they contemplate Hashem's greatness in Creation, they give birth to fear and love of Hashem.

catalogTitle: המוחין מולידות המדות' מחלוקת אם מהמוחין באים למדות או להיפך. החכמה והבינה עוסקים באהבה ויראה והדעת מקשרם למדות.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter three, the Mashgiach explains how chochmah and binah, the 'father and mother' of the mind, give birth to love and fear of Hashem through long, steady contemplation of His greatness, and why this was the Ba'al HaTanya's distinctive path.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter three: the first flash of an idea is chochmah, its development in length and breadth is binah, and they are called father and mother because their children are the middos, love and fear. This, he says, was the Ba'al HaTanya's distinctive view against most of the Maggid's other students, who worked with the public from the middos; both are true, and the dispute was over which path to teach the masses. With the mashal of a carpenter, he explains that a person was given a thinking soul in order to use it, and he describes the endless creation, worlds above worlds and angels above angels, whose contemplation brings first fear and then love. He shows this order in the brachos of Krias Shema, distinguishes fear of His exaltedness from fear of punishment, explains the language of longing through Shechem's hidden spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon, and concludes that only contemplation bound with da'as yields lasting love and fear.

en: Chochmah is the first point of an idea and binah its development; they are called father and mother because they give birth to the middos, love and fear of Hashem.
The Ba'al HaTanya held that avodah must start with contemplating G-dliness through chochmah, binah and da'as, while most of the Maggid's other students began with the middos.
Contemplating Hashem's greatness, a creation with no end and worlds and angels each as nothing before the one above it, brings a person first to fear of Hashem and then to love.
The yirah born of contemplation is fear of His exaltedness, awe before His greatness, not fear of punishment.
Da'as means binding: only strong, sustained contemplation bound to the mind gives love and fear permanence; otherwise they are 'shav', real but passing.

title.en: Chochmah and binah as father and mother

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter three: the first flash of an idea is chochmah, its development is binah, and they are father and mother whose children are love and fear. He explains that the Ba'al HaTanya held avodah must come through contemplating G-dliness with chochmah, binah and da'as, which then gives birth to the middos.

title.en: The dispute among the Maggid's students

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the difference of opinion between the Ba'al HaTanya and most of the Maggid's students, who began with the middos: both are true, and the question was how to teach the masses. He compares it to Yosef and his brothers, and to the dispute with Rabbi Mottel of Chernobyl over whether the Rebbe lifts the chassidim or they must lift themselves.

title.en: The thinking soul and the endless creation

summary.en: With the mashal of a carpenter who makes a table because he is a carpenter, the Mashgiach explains that a person was created with an intellect in order to use it. He then describes what contemplation reaches: a creation without end, the higher hidden worlds, and Hashem who fills and surrounds all worlds beyond even that.

title.en: Planets and angels: first fear, then love

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes the earth's orbit as a galgal that is nothing beside larger ones, and above them the souls and angels, each as nothing before the one above, up to the Kisei HaKavod. Such contemplation brings fear of Hashem and then love; he insists avodah must begin with fear, as Rosh Hashanah comes before Sukkos.

title.en: The order in the brachos of Krias Shema

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows the Tanya's order in the brachos of Krias Shema: Yotzer speaks of the luminaries and the angels and brings yirah, Ahavah Rabbah brings love, and then come Shema and Vehaya, the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven and of the mitzvos. He asks for whom Chazal instituted Yotzer if it is said in forty-five seconds without thought.

title.en: Fear of His exaltedness, not of punishment

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya's words, the Mashgiach explains that contemplation gives birth to fear of Hashem's exaltedness, unlike fear of punishment, which serves for reward. He compares it to the awe one feels before a great tzaddik, and explains the Tanya's word for shame through the Gemara that reads 'His fear upon your faces' as bushah.

title.en: Shechem's longing and the spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon

summary.en: After fear comes a burning love, and the Mashgiach notes that the Tanya's words of longing are those of the pesukim about Shechem and Dinah. Following the Midrash and the Ohr HaChaim, he explains that a hidden spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon in Shechem longed for its own kind, and so a Jew, a part of G-d, must long for Hashem; he adds that Rabbi Chanina was a gabbai tzedakah, a root of chesed.

title.en: Love from Abba, fear from Imma, and da'as

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that from chochmah, Abba, comes love, and from binah, Imma, comes fear, the two sides of right and left. He explains kelos hanefesh and the soul's thirst for Hashem from the element of fire, and that da'as means binding: the Ba'al HaTanya demands contemplation that is strong and sustained for long hours, not a moment.

title.en: Long davening and love that lasts

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls a talmid chacham in the Stoliner shul in Williamsburg who davened at length with contemplation and tears. Without da'as, he explains, love and fear are 'shav', not imaginary but without permanence; even passing life is worth something, yet the Ba'al HaTanya demands lasting life.

catalogTitle: Preparing for שבועות through Torah and Mitzvos

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches children that just as the shofar of Yovel returns every slave to his land and family, the fiftieth day, Shavuos, returns every Yid to his roots and to Hashem, and he urges them to prepare for it with Torah and teshuvah.

abstract.en: Speaking to children preparing for Shavuos, the Mashgiach first recalls the advice of a great mechanech, Rabbi Elias, never to be afraid of telling young boys something deep. He then explains that Hashem built laws into creation, like day and night or gravity, and that one such law is Yovel: everything must return to its source. Every Yid must return to Eretz Yisrael and to Hashem, which is the task of Moshiach and his shofar of freedom. Through the eved ivri of Parshas Mishpatim he contrasts the seventh year, when Hashem throws the drowning slave a rope, with the fiftieth year, when He dives in and pulls him out. Leaving Mitzrayim and counting seven times seven to Matan Torah follow the same pattern. Every Shavuos carries a scent of Yovel and a new Matan Torah, so the Mashgiach urges the children to do teshuvah, learn with diligence and beg Hashem for the true Yovel of Moshiach.

en: Hashem placed laws into creation, and one of them is that everything must return to the place it came from.
Yovel is the return of every Yid to his roots: to Eretz Yisrael, to his family and to Hashem, which Moshiach will bring with his shofar of freedom.
In the seventh year Hashem only throws the slave a rope, but in the fiftieth year He dives in and pulls him out whether he wants or not.
After Yetzias Mitzrayim the Yidden counted seven times seven, and the fiftieth day, like the fiftieth year, was Matan Torah with the sound of the shofar.
Every Shavuos there is a new Matan Torah and a reminder of Yovel; even one who cannot hear the shofar with his ears can hear it with his heart.
Shavuos must be prepared for, through Sefirah, teshuvah and the days of preparation, in order to receive one's portion in the Torah.

candidateTopics: Yovel and the shofar of freedom
laws of nature as Hashem's laws

title.en: Something deep, and the laws of creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the children that all success in Torah comes from Shavuos, recalls Rabbi Elias's advice not to fear telling young boys something deep, and begins with the laws Hashem built into nature: day and night, summer and winter, and the apple that falls to the ground.

title.en: Yovel: every Yid returns to his source

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains Yovel as a law of creation: as the apple returns to the ground, every Yid must return to Eretz Yisrael and to Hashem. This is the work of Moshiach, as the Rambam writes, and his shofar will proclaim freedom from the yetzer hara and return us to the state of Adam before the sin.

title.en: The rope and the lifeguard

summary.en: Through the eved ivri of Parshas Mishpatim, who loses his freedom and his place in the Jewish family, the Mashgiach contrasts the seventh year, when Hashem throws him a rope he may refuse, with Yovel, when Hashem dives in and pulls him out. He then applies the pattern to Mitzrayim, the counting of seven times seven and the shofar of Matan Torah.

title.en: Every Shavuos, a taste of Yovel

summary.en: The Mashgiach says Moshiach can come any day, and illustrates with a spinning penny that the chance stays even no matter how long we have waited. Even without Moshiach, every Shavuos carries a scent of Yovel and a new Matan Torah, and the shofar that cannot be heard with the ears can be heard with the heart.

title.en: Teshuvah and preparing for Matan Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the Yidden arrived at Sinai with teshuvah, and says that this teshuvah returns every Rosh Chodesh Sivan. The Torah commands preparing for Shavuos through Sefirah and the days of preparation, so he urges the children to learn with diligence and kavanah, do teshuvah and beg Hashem, and closes with a tefillah for the shofar of Moshiach.

catalogTitle: צריכים לעשות כל המצות במחשבה' דיבור ומעשה כדי שלא יהא הנשמה בעל מום.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew must fulfill all 613 mitzvos in thought, speech and deed so that no part of his soul remains blemished, and shows how one who cannot do so on his own can complete himself through Klal Yisrael and the tzaddik of the generation.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the three garments of the soul, thought, speech and deed, which correspond to neshamah, ruach and nefesh. The 613 mitzvos correspond to the 613 spiritual limbs of the soul, so a Jew must fulfill each of them in all three garments, or he must return in another gilgul to complete himself. For mitzvos one cannot perform, learning and speaking about them suffices; and he cites the Arizal's Sefer HaGilgulim. A further way is to join with Klal Yisrael, which forms one body with one comprehensive soul, the tzaddik of the generation. Just as one tzaddik includes all, one day includes all days, Yom Kippur, whose extension is Purim, and he tells of Mordechai appearing at a Purim seudah. Purim, he says, was made for the weak. He then reads the Tanya on pardes and closes on the mitzvos as garments of the soul, with the story of Reb Yitzchak Chayes.

en: Thought, speech and deed are the three garments of the soul, corresponding to neshamah, ruach and nefesh, so every mitzvah must be fulfilled in all three.
The 613 mitzvos correspond to the 613 limbs and sinews of the soul; one who has not fulfilled them all must return in a gilgul to complete himself.
For a mitzvah one has no opportunity to perform, it is enough to fulfill its thought and speech by learning and speaking about it.
Klal Yisrael is one body with one comprehensive soul, the tzaddik of the generation, and by binding oneself to him one can attain a tikkun even for mitzvos one did not fulfill.
Just as there is one tzaddik who includes all tzaddikim, there is one day that includes all days, Yom Kippur, and Purim is its extension, the tzaddik of the calendar.
The mitzvos a person does become garments for his soul in Olam Haba: learning clothes his mind, and doing mitzvos with love and fear clothes his middos.

candidateTopics: 613 mitzvos and the limbs of the soul
mitzvos as garments of the soul

title.en: Three garments and the 613 limbs of the soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that thought, speech and deed correspond to neshamah, ruach and nefesh, and that the 613 mitzvos correspond to the 613 spiritual limbs of the soul. One who leaves any mitzvah unfulfilled in all three garments must return in a gilgul; once is enough to complete that part of the soul.

title.en: Mitzvos one cannot perform; the Arizal on gilgul

summary.en: The Mashgiach says that for mitzvos one has no chance to do, such as pidyon haben, it suffices to learn and speak about them. He brings the Arizal in Sefer HaGilgulim that every person must fulfill the whole Torah in thought, speech and deed, and adds that one should not despair, since Moshiach is near.

title.en: Each Jew as a limb of Klal Yisrael

summary.en: The Mashgiach gives another way to the tikkun: joining with Klal Yisrael, which has one comprehensive soul. Each Jew is a limb of that body; one who learns is its head and one who davens is its heart, and through this unity one shares in the mitzvos others do.

title.en: The tzaddik of the generation as the general soul

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the comprehensive soul of Klal Yisrael is the tzaddik of the generation, Moshe Rabbeinu in his time and Mordechai in his. The tzaddik is revealed when the generation is worthy and hidden when not; the Gemara in Chagigah says the world stands on one tzaddik, and the main task of a Jew is to bind himself to him. He then turns to Sefer Yetzirah's division of world, year and soul.

title.en: Yom Kippur and Purim, the tzaddik of the calendar

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that as one tzaddik includes all tzaddikim, Yom Kippur includes all days and Yerushalayim includes all places. Yom Kippur has an extension, Purim, which he derives from the doubled 'achas bashanah'; Purim is even greater, and in the future Yom Kippur will be kept with pleasure as Purim is today.

title.en: Mordechai at every Purim; Purim for the weak

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a Purim seudah where a Jew who danced and sang was said to be Mordechai HaTzaddik, and explains from 'doresh tov le'amo' that Mordechai comes to every Jew's Purim. Purim, he says, was made for the weak and simple, whom Amalek attacked, not for the great ones who have the other Yamim Tovim.

title.en: Tikkun through the tzaddik; pardes and the soul

summary.en: Returning to the topic, the Mashgiach says that by binding oneself to the tzaddik who includes all souls one gains a tikkun for unfulfilled mitzvos. He reads the Tanya on deed, speech and thought in pardes, and explains that pshat, remez, drush and sod correspond to the levels of the soul, so one must strive to reach the sod of the Torah too.

title.en: Mitzvos as garments; Reb Yitzchak Chayes

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that thinking, speaking and doing Torah clothe the person in the Torah, and the mitzvos become his garments in Olam Haba. He tells how Reb Yitzchak Chayes appeared to his son in fine garments but barefoot, for lack of collecting tzedakah, and closes on Purim, when one should feel like a poor man before the Ribono shel Olam.

catalogTitle: מהתורה שלומד יש מזון לנשמה' ומהמצות שמקיים נעשה לבוש להנשמה. גדלות התורה לפי השגתו וגדלות נשמתו.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 4, the Mashgiach explains how Torah study clothes the soul like the mitzvos do, and why each Jew's share of that clothing depends on his understanding and on the root of his soul.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Tanya calls Torah a garment of the soul when it is usually called the soul's food, while the mitzvos are its garments. He answers that the Tanya speaks of the mitzvah side of Torah study, since learning is itself one of the 613 mitzvos. Using 'a mitzvah is a lamp and Torah is light', he shows that the two cannot be separated. He explains that tzitzis, sukkah and Shabbos include all the mitzvos, which is why a tallis has no sleeves, and that garments cost more than food just as mitzvos cost money while Torah is free. Torah clothes a person twice: it includes all the mitzvos, and it clothes his mind. With the story of the Apter Rav and the Rambam's letter, he teaches that each soul has a measured share in Torah, set by its root. He ends with the levels of time and Parshas Parah.

en: Torah is the soul's food and the mitzvos are its garments; the Tanya calls Torah study a garment because learning is also a mitzvah.
Torah and mitzvos cannot be separated: the mitzvah is the lamp and Torah is the light that rests on it.
Some mitzvos, like tzitzis, sukkah and Shabbos, include all the mitzvos, and Torah is also such an all-including mitzvah.
In the act and speech of a mitzvah all Jews are equal; the differences between them lie in the thought and kavanah behind it.
Each person has a measured portion in Torah, and how much holiness clothes him when he learns depends on the root of his soul.
Souls are rooted in different worlds and connected to different levels of Torah, but a great soul of pshat can be greater than a small soul of sod.
