the Rambam's letter to Rabbi Shmuel ibn Tibbon

title.en: Why Torah is called a garment

summary.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tanya's words that the soul is clothed in the 613 mitzvos, and asks why Torah is called a garment when it is the soul's food. He brings 'a mitzvah is a lamp and Torah is light' to show that Torah rests on the mitzvah and the two cannot be separated.

title.en: Tzitzis, the garment that includes all

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that learning Torah is also a mitzvah and so gives a garment, and that some mitzvos, like tzitzis, sukkah and Shabbos, include all the others. That is why a tallis, unlike a shirt or trousers, has no shape for any limb, and Rashi shows that tzitzis add up to 613.

title.en: Torah and mitzvah accompany each other

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that learning Torah is one of the 613 mitzvos in the Rambam's count, and that in a mitzvah the act is the main thing and Torah accompanies it, while in learning Torah is the main thing and the mitzvah accompanies it. He adds that garments cost more than food, just as mitzvos cost money while Torah is free.

title.en: Torah clothes the whole body and the mind

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya: in Torah study all 248 limbs are clothed in the 613 mitzvos, and the soul's ChaBaD is clothed in the Torah it understands. He explains the double garment: Torah includes all the mitzvos, as Chazal count 611 plus two, and it also clothes the mind that learns it.

title.en: Where Jews differ: kavanah and understanding

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that in the act and words of a mitzvah all Jews are equal: the Ba'al Shem Tov and a simple water carrier put on tefillin the same way. The difference lies in the kavanah, the love and fear that come from ChaBaD, and in Torah the clothing depends on how much a person understands and on his soul's root.

title.en: The Apter Rav and the Rambam's letter

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how the Ohev Yisroel, disturbed in his learning by crowds seeking blessings, asked his rebbe for permission to shut himself away, and was shown the Rambam's letter describing his exhausting day as the king's physician. He explains that Hashem gave the Rambam these burdens so that he would live long, since each person has a measured portion of Torah to complete.

title.en: Roots of souls and their share in Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that souls from Atzilus, such as Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the Arizal and the Ba'al Shem Tov, connect to sod, and souls of Beriah, Yetzirah and Asiyah to drush, remez and pshat. Yet the Beis Yosef, whose share the Arizal told him was halacha and pshat, was a giant soul, greater than a small soul of sod, and each Jew receives holiness from Torah according to the root of his soul.

title.en: Adar, Parshas Parah and Purim

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the order from head to heel to time: Nissan is the head of the year and Adar its lowest point, which is why the Megillah has no name of Hashem. Parshas Parah, read on the last Shabbos of Adar, belongs to that low point: no one knows its reason and only its pshat and halachos can be learned, and it is a tikkun for the lowly, like Purim.

catalogTitle: כשלומד תורה משיג אלקות' ויש יחוד בינו ובין ה' יותר מבעוה"ב .

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains how a Jew who learns Torah and does mitzvos truly grasps and unites with Hashem Himself, because Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the halachos, a union greater than anything in Olam Haba.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach returns to the Tanya's claim that through Torah and mitzvos all ten faculties of the soul unite with Hashem, and asks how this is possible when Hashem is the Ein Sof whom no thought can grasp. Intellect, he explains, is simply not the sense that perceives Hashem. The answer is tzimtzum: Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the mitzvos and their halachos, as a scientist carries radioactive material in a lead container. How much light a person receives depends on how he learns. The Torah descended like water, level by level, until it was clothed in thought, speech and physical action. After a long digression on the body as the seat of the ten faculties and on refining the middos during Sefirah, he explains why one hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world exceeds all of Olam Haba, and closes with the parable of embracing the king.

en: Hashem is beyond all grasp of thought, not because human intellect is too weak but because intellect is not the sense that perceives Him.
Hashem contracted His will and wisdom into the 613 mitzvos and their halachos, so that one who understands a halachah grasps Hashem Himself, clothed in a garment.
How much divine light fills the vessel of Torah depends on how the person learns: with fear of Heaven and honor for the Torah, or lightheadedly.
The Torah descended like water from its high place, level by level through the worlds, until it was clothed in physical things, so that every thought, word and action can take hold of it.
One hour of Torah and mitzvos in this world exceeds all of Olam Haba, because there one enjoys only the radiance of the Shechinah, while here one is united with Hashem Himself.

title.en: How can one unite with the Ein Sof?

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls that through Torah and mitzvos all faculties of the soul unite with Hashem, and asks how this can be when Hashem is the Ein Sof whom no thought grasps. He explains that intellect is not the sense for perceiving Hashem, as a watch cannot understand its maker, and that even His will and wisdom are beyond understanding.

title.en: Hashem's wisdom contracted into the halachos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Tanya that where one finds Hashem's greatness one finds His humility: He contracted His will and wisdom into the mitzvos and halachos. With the parable of radioactive material carried in a lead container, he explains that one who understands a halachah holds Hashem Himself in his mind, clothed in garments, and that the lowest halachos hold the greatest holiness.

title.en: Each word of Torah is a vessel for light

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every word of Torah is a vessel that holds divine light, and how much light enters depends on the learner. One who learns with fear of Heaven and honor receives the light; one who learns lightheadedly has an empty vessel; even learning not for its own sake, aiming to reach lishmah, has its place, and great tzaddikim drew great powers from their Torah.

title.en: The Torah descends like water

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads on in the Tanya: Hashem contracted Himself into the mitzvos so that every mind can grasp them, and the ten faculties of the soul are clothed in the three garments of thought, speech and action. He explains the Midrash comparing Torah to water that flows to the lowest place, the chain of worlds down to parchment and ink, and how the ten faculties correspond to the parts of the body, as in Pesach Eliyahu.

title.en: Refining the middos in the days of Sefirah

summary.en: In a digression, the Mashgiach explains that during the weeks of Sefirah one refines the middos, which are rooted in the limbs of the body, so as to receive the Torah on Shavuos. He shows that the laws of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah fall in the sedras read in these weeks, and brings Rabbi Chaim Vital that without good middos one cannot receive the Torah, along with Pirkei Avos and the Bnei Yissaschar.

title.en: Greater than all of Olam Haba

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that through Torah and mitzvos the whole body is wrapped in the 'bundle of life' with Hashem, and therefore Chazal say one hour in this world is better than all of Olam Haba. In Olam Haba one enjoys only the radiance of the Shechinah, like the sun's rays, while here Hashem gives Himself in tangible form through physical mitzvos.

title.en: Embracing the King through His garments

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's parable of one who embraces the king: though the king is clothed in garments, it is truly the king he embraces. He brings 'His right hand embraces me' and 'Let Him kiss me with the kisses of His mouth', asks why the passuk says the right hand, and answers that Torah comes from chesed and water, which is the right side. He concludes that the union of this world exceeds that of Olam Haba.

catalogTitle: Fulfilling the Destiny of כלל ישראל - to Return to their Roots - the אבות

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Yovel, Shavuos and the final Geulah all mean a return of Klal Yisrael to its roots, the level of the Avos, and that every Jew, even the lowest, carries a hidden point that will one day be brought back.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Ramban that the Geulah from Mitzrayim was complete only at Har Sinai, when the Jews returned to the level of the Avos, and calls this return Yovel. Shabbos and Shemitah are a return that one may refuse; Yom Kippur and Yovel pull everyone back. Following Rashi's question on Shemitah and Sinai, he links Yovel to the fiftieth day, Shavuos, and to the fiftieth level, which is hidden, as shown by the third-person 'hotzeisi osam' and the last word of Ana Bekoach, 'taalumos'. He then asks why the kedushah of Yosef and Serach protected all of Klal Yisrael but not Shlomis bas Divri, whose son the Arizal identifies with Yeshu. Her son needed the fiftieth level; yet even he has a good point, as the Gemara shows. The Mashgiach ties Yovel to hashavas aveidah, Rus's return, Rachel in Beis Lechem with a story, and the indelible point in every Jew.

en: According to the Ramban, the Geulah from Mitzrayim was completed at Har Sinai, when Klal Yisrael returned to the level of the Avos, and the final Geulah will restore that level fully.
Shabbos and Shemitah are a return that a person can decline, while Yom Kippur and Yovel bring everyone back, even against his will.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is Yovel and the fiftieth level, a level that is hidden and beyond the reach of the klalos and the sitra achra.
Every Jew, even the worst, has a hidden good point that never wanted to leave Hashem, and Yovel will bring it back to its root.
Yovel and Shemitah are a branch of the mitzvah of returning a lost object: everything lost goes back to its original owner.

title.en: The Geulah as a return to the Avos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Ramban that the Geulah from Mitzrayim was completed at Sinai, when the Jews returned to the level of the Avos, and calls this return Yovel. He contrasts Shabbos and Shemitah, which one may refuse, with Yom Kippur and Yovel, which bring everyone back.

title.en: Shemitah, Sinai and the fiftieth level

summary.en: From Rashi's question why Shemitah is tied to Sinai, the Mashgiach links Yovel to Shavuos, the fiftieth day, and to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who finds the good point in every Jew. He brings the Zohar on the fifty mentions of yetzias Mitzrayim, the Ramak that the fiftieth is in this week's sedra, and explains why it is said in the third person.

title.en: Taalumos, and Shlomis bas Divri

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the last word of Ana Bekoach, 'taalumos', is the hidden fiftieth level revealed at the end of Sefirah, and mentions the Arizal's custom on haircuts. He then turns to Shlomis bas Divri, whose son the Arizal identifies with Yeshu, and to the kedushah of Yosef and Serach that protected Klal Yisrael in Mitzrayim.

title.en: Why the kedushah stopped short at Shlomis

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the kedushah of Yosef and Serach did not reach Shlomis, and answers that her son needed the fiftieth level, which they did not reach. He brings what he heard, that every Jew returns to his root after fifty thousand Yovlos, and shows from the Gemara about Onkelos and about Yehoshua ben Perachya that even Yeshu had good in him.

title.en: Yehuda and Dan in the Mishkan

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings Rashi that the Mishkan was built by Betzalel of Yehuda, the foremost tribe, and Oholiav of Dan, the lowest, and that Nachshon ben Aminadav and Shlomis bas Divri are equal in gematria. In the hidden point even the biggest rasha is not a rasha, though it takes fifty thousand Yovlos to free it.

title.en: Yovel as hashavas aveidah; Rus returns

summary.en: The Mashgiach calls Shemitah and Yovel a branch of the mitzvah of returning a lost object, brings the Baal HaTurim on the root 'geulah' in the sedra, and explains that Shavuos is the return of what was lost. He asks how Rus could 'return' to a land she had never been in, and connects Beis Lechem and Rachel Imeinu to the mitzvah of Yovel.

title.en: Rachel Imeinu at the bris

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells a story he heard through Rav Mati Finkelman: a woman who was blessed with a child after davening at Kever Rachel invited Rachel to the bris, and an unknown woman of great beauty who appeared in every photograph came out blank in all of them.

title.en: The indelible point and every Jew's portion

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the shofar of Yovel and the point in every Jew that cries 'rotzeh ani', which remains even in those who have no share in Olam Haba, and brings Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's claim to exempt the world from judgment. He closes with every Jew's letter in the Torah and portion in Eretz Yisrael, and with Sefirah as earning by oneself what was given on Pesach.

catalogTitle: כל אחד זוכה להאור שבתורה לפי קדושתו ומדרגתו.

oneLiner.en: Building on the Derech Hashem and Tanya chapter 5, the Mashgiach explains that Torah draws down G-dliness only when learned with awe and by an upright Jew, each according to his level, and that understanding a halacha unites a person with Hashem's wisdom more deeply than any other mitzvah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach recalls from chapter 4 that Torah and mitzvos are vessels for Hashem's light, and brings the Derech Hashem: every person, through Torah and mitzvos, draws holy influence into himself and into all creation, but on two conditions. The first is learning with seriousness and derech eretz, not lightheadedly; here he discusses dress while learning, tells of the Arugas Habosem, and warns against copying a rebbe's faults, citing the four kinds of students in Avos. The second is being an upright Jew, though even a rasha's Torah keeps a trace of holiness. After the parable of the esrog, he learns Tanya chapter 5: the intellect grasps what it understands and is enclothed in it, so understanding a halacha grasps Hashem's will, a unity greater than any mitzvah. He compares sod and pshat, explains Torah as the soul's bread, and closes with a story from R' Yitzchak Chayes.

en: Through Torah and mitzvos every Jew draws holy influence into himself and into all of creation, each according to the reach of his soul.
According to the Derech Hashem, Torah draws down holiness only when learned with awe, seriousness and derech eretz, and by a person who is not a rasha.
Words of Torah are vessels for G-dliness, like a lamp that gives light only when connected to the current.
Even Torah learned without the proper way keeps some holiness of its own, like a body that keeps a trace of the soul.
Tanya chapter 5 teaches that when one understands a halacha, his intellect grasps Hashem's will and is enclothed in it, a two-way unity found in no physical thing.
The unity of Torah study surpasses that of mitzvos: a mitzvah enclothes a person from outside, while Torah is taken inside, like bread that becomes part of the body.

candidateTopics: conditions for Torah study to draw holiness
derech eretz and yiras shamayim in learning
Torah as a vessel for G-dliness
unity of the intellect with the halacha
Torah as bread of the soul

title.en: Torah and mitzvos draw light into all creation

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls chapter 4, that Torah and mitzvos are vessels for Hashem's holiness, and brings the Derech Hashem: through them each person draws holy influence into himself and into all creation, some tzaddikim to the point of bringing a city, a country or the world to teshuvah.

title.en: First condition: learning with awe; the Arugas Habosem

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Derech Hashem's first condition, that Torah be learned with seriousness and awe, not sprawled out lightheadedly, and discusses how people dress while learning. He tells how a fellow student found the Arugas Habosem learning on a hot day fully dressed, and the Arugas Habosem answered that he had learned other things from their Rebbe.

title.en: Learning the good from a rebbe, not the faults

summary.en: Using the four kinds of students in Avos, the Mashgiach warns against picking out a rebbe's apparent faults, such as the Ohev Yisroel's eating or R' Baruch's anger, which had hidden reasons. He explains that chassidim in Eretz Yisroel learn in shirtsleeves because of the hot climate of their origins, while the common rule is derech eretz for Torah.

title.en: Respect for seforim; the lamp and the current

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Derech Hashem that one must honor the seforim and speak respectfully of the Rishonim; learning without derech eretz draws nothing. Torah words are vessels in which Hashem contracts Himself, and like a lamp not plugged in, they give no light when learned without awe.

title.en: Second condition; each according to his level; the esrog

summary.en: The second condition is that the learner not be a rasha, yet even a rasha's Torah has a trace of holiness that brings him back, like a body that keeps a trace of its soul; each person draws according to his level. The Mashgiach then explains why an esrog worth twenty cents costs a hundred and fifty dollars: G-dliness is enclothed in it, so holding it one holds G-dliness.

title.en: Tanya ch. 5: intellect, knower and known

summary.en: The Mashgiach begins Tanya chapter 5 on the term 'grasping', and explains the three terms sechel, maskil and muskal. The intellect grasps and surrounds what it understands, and at the same time is enclothed in it, as one absorbed in a Tosfos does not hear when called: a two-way unity.

title.en: Halacha as Hashem's will; a wondrous unity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every halacha, even about cases that may never occur, is Hashem's wisdom and will; when one understands it clearly, he grasps what no thought can grasp, like embracing the king through his garments. This is a unity with nothing like it in the physical world, greater than that of mitzvos, which enclothe a person only from outside.

title.en: Mitzvos with kavanah; sod versus pshat

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that a mitzvah done with kavanah also includes Torah, but the Tanya speaks of the bare act. He then explains that each grasps Torah according to his intellect in pshat, remez, drash and sod: sod is higher because it has fewer garments, yet a clearly understood Gemara gives a stronger unity, since no one fully grasps the secrets of the Torah.

title.en: Torah as bread; mitzvos as garments

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains why Torah is called bread that nourishes the soul when learned in depth, and brings the Zohar that in the world of souls Torah is food and mitzvos are garments. He brings R' Pinchas of Koretz on why mitzvos cost money and Torah is free, tells of R' Yitzchak Chayes who appeared to his son in fine garments but without shoes, and closes urging both collecting for Jews and learning Torah lishmah.

catalogTitle: עשר כתרין דמסאבותא כנגד עשר ספירות דקדושה. ביאור טעם שהטומאה נקראת כתרין.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter six, the Mashgiach explains that the ten powers of kedushah have a counterpart of ten 'crowns' of impurity, why impurity is called crowns and sitra achra, and how a Jew elevates kelipas noga by doing even permitted things for the sake of Heaven.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the principle 'zeh l'umas zeh asah ha'Elokim': Hashem keeps kedushah and impurity in balance, and only one who takes Hashem with him tips the scale. He illustrates this with the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya, a Midrash about the Satan at the births of the Avos, and the great sorcerers of earlier times. He then reads Tanya chapter six: just as the G-dly soul has ten holy sefiros, the Jew's animal soul from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity. Using a walnut's four shells, the laws of orlah, milah and periah, and the Masorah's siman for Parshas Kedoshim, he shows that only a Jew can elevate noga. He explains why impurity is called 'crowns' rather than sefiros, how intellect shapes the middos, why there is no neutral reshus, and, with a vort of the Kotzker Rebbe, why impurity is called the 'other side'.

en: Hashem made kedushah and impurity in balance, 'zeh l'umas zeh'; only by taking Hashem along does a person tip the balance toward kedushah.
Just as the G-dly soul has ten holy sefiros clothed in thought, speech and action, the animal soul from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity: seven bad middos and an intellect divided into three.

A Jew's animal soul is from kelipas noga, which can be turned to kedushah when he eats and does physical things for the sake of Heaven; a gentile's comes from the three wholly impure kelipos, which cannot.
Impurity is called 'crowns' and not sefiros because a sefirah is transparent and nullified to Hashem, while each power of impurity declares 'I will reign'.
There is no neutral middle: a permitted act not done for Heaven's sake joins the side of impurity, which is why it is called sitra achra, the 'other side'.

candidateTopics: eating for the sake of Heaven

title.en: Zeh l'umas zeh: kedushah and impurity in balance

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the previous perek on the union with Hashem through Torah and mitzvos, then opens chapter six with 'zeh l'umas zeh asah ha'Elokim'. He brings the Gemara about Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya and the minim, and concludes that kedushah and impurity are balanced, and Hashem tips the scale for one who takes Him along.

title.en: The Satan's share, Esav and the great sorcerers

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings a Midrash that the Satan demanded a share at the births of the Avos, and that Esav, the admoni, was born with Yaakov; David too was admoni, but with fine eyes. He then explains that when there were great tzaddikim there were also great sorcerers like Bilaam and Amalek, while today both sides are small, and that a union exists in impurity as in kedushah.

title.en: Ten sefiros of the soul and ten of impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the opening of Tanya chapter six: as the G-dly soul consists of ten sefiros clothed in three garments, the soul of the sitra achra from kelipas noga has ten powers of impurity, seven bad middos with a mind that gives birth to them. He mentions that in the days of sefirah one asks to refine each middah through the mitzvah of counting.

title.en: Kelipas noga: the walnut, orlah and periah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that a Jew's animal soul is from kelipas noga, which can be elevated, and illustrates the four kelipos with the four shells of a walnut. He shows the same pattern in 'kedoshim tihyu' as the Ramban explains it, in orlah and its fourth year, and in milah and periah, and notes that the Masorah's siman for the 64 pesukim of Parshas Kedoshim is 'noga'.

title.en: Bnei Keturah: milah without periah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Rambam that the Bnei Keturah are obligated in milah, and the Acharonim who say only milah and not periah, since periah was given only in the days of Yehoshua. The inner reason is that a gentile's soul comes from the three impure kelipos and cannot elevate noga, which is also why only a Jew brings shelamim, as the Midrash on 'uri tzafon' shows.

title.en: Why impurity is called 'crowns'

summary.en: The Mashgiach rereads the Tanya and asks why the ten powers of impurity are called crowns and not sefiros. A sefirah, like 'livnas hasapir', is transparent and lets the light of kedushah through, which is bittul; impurity says 'I am something' and 'I will reign'. He links the ten powers of impurity to the ten sons of Haman.

title.en: The mind behind the middos; garments of impurity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya's point that the middos follow the intellect: a child and an adult have the same middah of love, but a small mind directs it to toys and a large one to property. He then explains the three garments of impurity, thought, speech and action not for Hashem, and 'all that is done under the sun', which is futility and a broken spirit.

title.en: No neutral reshus: the 'other side'

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that there is no middle between mitzvah and aveirah: eating or business done for Heaven's sake raises noga to kedushah, and otherwise it joins impurity. He brings the Kotzker Rebbe on the Targum's 'l'tzad' in 'al tigshu el ishah', that there are two sides of a fence, and concludes with the Tanya that kedushah rests only on what is nullified to Hashem.

catalogTitle: ישראל בטל לה' בעצם' ומקבל מצד הקדושה' הסיטרא אחרא ישות ואינו בטל לה'' ומקבל בבחינת אחוריים.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains, on Tanya chapter 6, that holiness is whatever is nullified to Hashem and receives from Him face to face, while the sitra achra is self-standing 'something' that receives its life only from behind and in hiding.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Tanya's teaching that the Shechinah rests on ten Jews, because ten is the number of bitul: in a minyan each Jew loses his separate identity and becomes part of one unit. He supports this from the numbers of the tribes, which always ended in tens and hundreds, and from the minyan being learned from the meraglim, explaining that only the good part of Jews joins together, while evil, like the goyim, cannot unite, since holiness is unity and klipah is separation. He then explains that whatever says 'I am something' occupies space and pushes Hashem away, as with the ba'al ga'avah, unlike the Aron that took up no space. Hashem gives life to everything at every moment, but to the sitra achra only from behind, through man, who is a small world. He ends with the two levels of klipos, the three impure ones and klipas nogah, shown in the walnut, milah, orlah, the siddur and Yechezkel's vision.

en: The Shechinah rests on ten Jews because in a minyan each one is nullified and they become one unit of holiness.
Holiness is unity and klipah is separation, so only the good part of Jews can join together, and evil, even ten wrongdoers together, never forms a minyan.
Whoever considers himself 'something' occupies space and pushes Hashem away, so the revelation of Hashem is absent from him, measure for measure.
Hashem creates the world anew at every moment, and even the klipos and the wicked receive their life from Him, only in hiding.
Holiness receives face to face, while the sitra achra receives from 'behind', through a long descent of contractions.
Man, made in the image of G-d, is a small world, and through him the shefa reaches all of creation, including the sitra achra.
The klipos have two levels: three wholly impure ones that must be cut off, and klipas nogah, which can be subdued and turned to holiness.

candidateTopics: holiness as unity and klipah as separation
klipas nogah and the three impure klipos

title.en: Ten as the number of bitul

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that the Shechinah rests on ten, because there the Jews are nullified into one. He explains why the four compartments of tefillin are learned from foreign languages, and that ten is written as one with a zero, the many nullified to the one.

title.en: Ten Jews, the tribes and the meraglim

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the saying that where ten Jews are, even without learning Torah, angels cannot enter, and ties ten to the ten utterances of creation. He shows that the census of the tribes always ended in tens, and asks why the minyan is learned from the wicked meraglim.

title.en: Holiness unites, klipah separates

summary.en: The Mashgiach answers that in ten Jews each loses his identity and they form one unit, which goyim cannot do, since klipah is a world of separation. Only the good part of each Jew joins, as the chelbonah in the ketores shows, and so even the meraglim formed a minyan through their inner good.

title.en: The proud man occupies space

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads that whatever is not nullified does not receive from the inner holiness. Hashem fills every place, but He is revealed only where there is bitul; the ba'al ga'avah who says 'I am something' occupies space, unlike the Aron, which miraculously took up no space, and so Hashem leaves him, measure for measure.

title.en: Constant creation, like electricity

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that even where the sitra achra is, Hashem's kingship is there in hiding, since He creates the world anew at every moment, as electricity must be generated constantly for a lamp to burn. Even klipos, wild animals and the wicked receive shefa at every moment, but with hester panim.

title.en: Face to face and from behind

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts the face-to-face bond of holiness with giving over the shoulder to someone one does not like. He reads the Tanya that what is not nullified receives only from 'behind', through descent upon descent and contraction upon contraction, until it can exist as a separate thing.

title.en: Man as a small world

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that man holds the key to creation and channels shefa to it through his mitzvos, his 248 limbs and 365 sinews matching the mitzvos. Man is a microcosm: his face forms Hashem's name, his mouth is a patach, the vowel of chochmah, and the world in turn has eyes, a mouth and a heart, Yerushalayim.

title.en: How the sitra achra is fed

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the sitra achra also needs sustenance, and it receives from 'behind', from the waste left when the good of food is separated, in the place where holiness cannot be. Deep within are sparks of holiness in exile, like the Jews in galus, and therefore this world is called the world of klipos, with only islands of holiness.

title.en: The two levels of klipos

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that in this world evil is the majority and holiness the minority. He explains the three impure klipos and klipas nogah through the four layers of a walnut, milah, orlah, the nusach of Velamalshinim and Yechezkel's vision, and closes with wishes for receiving the Torah with joy.

catalogTitle: חרות על הלוחות - Free Yourself from the Bondages of your יצר הרע

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach teaches young bachurim that Shavuos, the fiftieth day like the Yovel year, proclaims true freedom: freedom from slavery to the yetzer hara, which a person receives anew each year by preparing to accept the Torah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the eved Ivri, the Jewish slave who goes free in his seventh year but may choose to stay a slave, until the shofar of the fiftieth year, Yovel, frees everyone. In the same way, the Ramban explains that leaving Mitzrayim was only freedom from physical labor; the Jews became truly free fifty days later, at Har Sinai. The Mashgiach then shows what slavery really is through a seventeen-year-old who celebrates his eighteenth birthday with a pack of cigarettes, thinking he is free, while he is a slave to his yetzer hara; the same holds for late-night television and the internet. Charus al haluchos: the Luchos give freedom, but Shavuos needs preparation more than any other day, from the counting to Akdamus. A story of the Sanzer Rav's son shows that Matan Torah can be seen again. Shavuos is no commemoration like the Fourth of July: every year Hashem gives the Torah anew, and each person must receive it.

en: Just as the Yovel shofar frees every eved Ivri, even the one who wanted to stay a slave, the fiftieth day of Shavuos is the day of freedom for the Jewish people.

Following the Ramban, the Mashgiach explains that leaving Mitzrayim ended only physical bondage; true freedom means returning to the level of the Avos with the Shechinah upon them, reached fifty days later.
A person who does what his yetzer hara demands, against his own logic and his neshamah, is a slave, however free he imagines himself to be.
Charus al haluchos: the Luchos received on the fiftieth day are what give a person freedom.
No day in the Jewish calendar requires as much preparation as Shavuos, and the preparation runs from the counting through the night of learning to Akdamus.
Shavuos is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July: every year Hashem gives the Torah anew, and each person must do his part of kabbalas haTorah.
Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah for ruchniyus, a day of judgment for Torah, tefillah and middos, just as Rosh Hashanah in Tishrei is for gashmiyus.

title.en: The eved Ivri who refuses freedom

summary.en: The Mashgiach praises the bachurim for gathering to prepare for Shavuos, then turns to the parshiyos of Shemitah and Yovel: the eved Ivri goes free in his personal seventh year, his Shabbos, yet one wretched slave declares he wants to stay in chains.

title.en: Yovel, the Ramban and the fiftieth day

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the shofar of Yovel on Yom Kippur frees even the slave who wanted to stay. He brings the Ramban that leaving Mitzrayim was only freedom from physical labor, and that the Jews became free fifty days later; Sefirah parallels Shemitah and Yovel, and the shofar at Har Sinai proclaimed their freedom.

title.en: The boy who celebrates freedom with cigarettes

summary.en: To explain what freedom means, the Mashgiach describes a seventeen-year-old who is not allowed to smoke and on his eighteenth birthday flashes a pack of cigarettes as proof he is free. Pointing to the Surgeon General's warning and the years smokers lose, he shows that the boy is really a slave to his yetzer hara, fooling himself that one cigarette does no harm.

title.en: The crying neshamah: television and internet

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew's neshamah comes from heaven and protests inside him after an aveirah, but the slave of the yetzer hara cannot listen. He illustrates this with a boy kept up watching television until late at night instead of chazering, and with another who logs onto the internet and is dragged into filth while his yetzer tov begs him to break free.

title.en: Charus al haluchos and preparing for Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Mishnah in Pirkei Avos, charus al haluchos, read on the Shabbos before Shavuos: the Luchos received on the fiftieth day give freedom. He stresses that no day requires as much preparation as Shavuos and lists the stages: counting fifty days, the three days of preparation, staying up the night of Shavuos, and Akdamus, a lesson in emunah, before the Aseres Hadibros are heard.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav's son sees Matan Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells how Rav Chatzkel of Shinava, son of the Divrei Chaim of Sanz, spent Shavuos with Rav Shalom of Belz and beheld Matan Torah at the reading of the Torah. The next year his father kept him home and showed it to him himself, explaining that he had held back so his son would grow to see it with his own strength.

title.en: Matan Torah every year, not a commemoration

summary.en: The Mashgiach says one who believes it will feel that every Shavuos gives the Torah anew, and distinguishes Matan Torah from kabbalas haTorah, which depends on a person's desire. Contrasting the Fourth of July, a mere commemoration, he explains that Shavuos is a yearly rerun of Matan Torah and a Rosh Hashanah for ruchniyus, urges preparation through learning and davening, and closes with a brachah for true freedom.

catalogTitle: קליפת נוגה יכול להתהפך לטוב; ענינים גשמיים יכולים להתהפך לטוב.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains why the body, food and worldly matters of a Jew, which come from klipas nogah, can be turned to holiness, while what comes from the three wholly impure klipos cannot.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the haftarah of Shavuos, where Yechezkel passes through four layers before the vision; the letter vav before 'nogah' marks it as a different kind of klipah, like the edible fourth peel of a nut. From the Tanya he explains that the body and animal soul of a gentile come from the three impure klipos, which cannot be elevated, while a Jew's body and kosher food come from nogah, which can; this is why only olos are accepted from gentiles. The inanimate world is not listed among the impure klipos because earth is batel to Hashem, as shown by the Girgashi and by Avraham's dust on erev Pesach. He then shows that the psak of the chachamim decides whether a thing falls into the impure klipos, and that even reality follows the Torah's psak. Finally, from Tanya ch. 7, he explains that eating, business, a joke or a vacation done for the sake of Heaven are raised to holiness.

en: Klipas nogah differs in kind from the three wholly impure klipos: what comes from it can be turned to good, while the three klipos cannot.
A gentile's body and animal soul come from the three impure klipos, so he can bring only an olah, while a Jew can eat meat for the sake of Heaven and bring shelamim.
The inanimate is not counted among the three impure klipos, because earth, the level of malchus, is batel to Hashem.
Whether something falls into the impure klipos depends on how the chachamim rule, and even physical reality follows the Torah's psak.
Permitted worldly acts such as eating, business or sleep become holiness when done for the sake of Heaven, and otherwise are no better than the animal soul itself.

title.en: The four klipos and the vav before nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach opens with Yechezkel's vision from the Shavuos haftarah and the four layers he passes through, compares them to the four peels of a nut, and explains that nogah alone can be turned to holiness. He shows this with the rule that only olos are accepted from gentiles, the Midrash about the chazir in the future, and the nesachim the Jews prepared from the meraglim's fruit.

title.en: Tanya ch. 6: the two levels of klipah

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares nogah to the priah of a bris, which is not cut off but folded back, then reads the Tanya on the two levels of klipah. He explains that the souls of gentiles and forbidden foods from the inanimate, plants and animals come from the three impure klipos, while a Jew's body, kosher food and permitted matters like business and health come from nogah.

title.en: Why the inanimate is not in the impure klipos

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that the Tanya lists plants, animals and people among the three impure klipos but not the inanimate. He explains that the inanimate is malchus, earth, which is batel to Hashem, as Avraham called himself dust and ashes, and that the Girgashi, the nation opposite malchus, left the land on its own.

title.en: Avraham's dust against the kings on erev Pesach

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells the Midrash that Og came to Avraham on erev Pesach while he baked matzos, and that Avraham fought the four kings into the night by throwing dust at them. He explains that dust is bitul, like bitul chametz, and this is how one nullifies the yetzer hara and the klipos.

title.en: The chacham's psak decides, and Reb Chaim Ozer's advice

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that when a question arises, Heaven rules as the chacham rules, so one should daven about it, as Dovid HaMelech did about his status. He tells how Reb Chaim Ozer advised a man with a lung illness to move to Eretz Yisroel, where the Beis Yosef's lenient ruling is followed, and he lived; every machlokes reflects different heavenly halls, and both views are true.

title.en: Reality follows the Torah's psak

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the mishnah in Niddah on the inner organs, where Rashi, Tosfos and the Rambam each describe the anatomy differently, and the Chasam Sofer's statement that reality matches the Rambam. He explains that the Torah is the blueprint of the world, each opinion has its place in Heaven, and since the halachah follows the Rambam, the anatomy follows him; he adds Rashi's comment on the missing yud in 'nesi'im'.

title.en: Nature changes with the chachamim's chiddushim

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that nature changes from generation to generation, with new illnesses and remedies, and brings Tosfos on a mishnah about the age at which a cow gives birth. Since nature follows the Torah's chiddushim, he explains why the Gemara sends one with a sick person to a chacham: a tzaddik cannot change the Torah, but a chacham can, through a chiddush, change the psak and with it the order of creation.

title.en: Tanya ch. 7: worldly acts for the sake of Heaven

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya ch. 7 and explains that even eating kosher food, talking or doing business is nogah, which tips like a scale to holiness when done for the sake of Heaven, and otherwise is no better than the animal soul. He adds that in this world evil is the majority, from insects to people.

title.en: Good meat, wine and a joke before learning

summary.en: The Mashgiach continues the Tanya: nogah is an intermediate level, and someone who eats fine meat and drinks wine to broaden his mind for Torah and mitzvos elevates them. Likewise a joke said to open the heart before learning, as Rabbah did before his students, is raised to holiness, unlike empty levity.

title.en: A vacation for the sake of Heaven

summary.en: Ending the season of Tanya, the Mashgiach speaks about going to the country: seeing Hashem's natural world brings a person contentment and awareness of His greatness. A vacation taken to broaden the mind for avodah raises all of nature to holiness, and one taken otherwise drags it down to the impure klipos.

catalogTitle: לכל יהודי יש חלק בתורה מיוחד לו; טעם שמתוך שלא לשמה בא לשמה.

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that every Jew has his own portion in the Torah and a hidden inner point of closeness to Hashem, and that this hidden point is why learning not for its own sake leads to learning lishmah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's definition of Torah lishmah: learning in order to bind one's soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, each according to his intellect, and contrasts it with the Nefesh HaChaim's definition of learning to understand. Since every Jewish soul is rooted in the Torah, each person is drawn to particular parts of it. This leads him to the levels of pshat, remez, drush and sod, and to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who revealed the hidden part of the Torah. Every Jew, too, carries a sod: a hidden grace before Hashem that no one else knows. He illustrates this with Pesach Sheni, the people who were tamei who still asked why they should be left out, and their link to Nadav and Avihu, Pinchas and Lag BaOmer. Returning to the Tanya, he explains that a hidden point of lishmah lies within every act done not lishmah. He ends with the Tanya's teaching that Torah is food and garment, while mitzvos are garments alone.

en: According to the Tanya, learning Torah lishmah means learning in order to bind one's soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, each according to his intellect.
Every Jewish soul is rooted in the Torah, so each person feels a desire for the particular part of the Torah where his soul is rooted.
Just as the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, every Jew carries a sod: a hidden grace before Hashem that only Hashem knows.
The people who were tamei on Pesach Sheni could ask why they should be left out because their inner point is untouched by tumah, and in that hidden place all Jews are equal.
Learning not lishmah leads to lishmah because within every act not done lishmah lies a hidden point that wants to do it lishmah, and Hashem knows it.
Torah is food and also a garment for the soul, while mitzvos are only garments that surround a person from outside.

candidateTopics: each soul's portion in the Torah
Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and Lag BaOmer
the hidden point of every Jew
Torah as food and mitzvos as garments

title.en: Lishmah and each soul's portion in Torah

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya's definition of lishmah, binding the soul to Hashem through grasping the Torah, and contrasts it with the Nefesh HaChaim. He explains that every soul is rooted in the Torah, so each person is drawn to a particular part of it, and nowadays a person carries sparks of many souls whose desires change over the years.

title.en: The levels of Torah and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the Torah has levels of pshat, remez, drush and sod, and that some souls belong to its inner part, the portion of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai. Rashbi dug out and revealed the hidden part of the Torah, which will be the main learning when Moshiach comes, and this is the idea of Lag BaOmer.

title.en: Every Jew carries a secret

summary.en: Since every Jew is a letter in the Torah, he too has pshat, remez, drush and sod; his sod is a hidden grace before Hashem that no one else has, even when outwardly he looks like a sinner. The Mashgiach brings the Chiddushei HaRim on this and the Beis Aharon that every Jew can find chizuk in Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

title.en: Chesed shebehod and the claim of Pesach Sheni

summary.en: The Mashgiach notes that today is chesed shebehod, the start of the week of hod, which already carries the power of Lag BaOmer. He turns to the people who were tamei from a dead body and asked why they should be left out of the korban Pesach, and explains the halachos about who may not enter the camps.

title.en: Nadav and Avihu, Pinchas and Eliyahu

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the people who were tamei had dealt with Nadav and Avihu, whose souls entered Pinchas, and Pinchas is Eliyahu. He asks why the passuk calls Pinchas the son of Elazar the son of Aharon HaKohen again, and answers that with Nadav and Avihu's souls he became also a son of Aharon.

title.en: The hidden point no tumah reaches

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the people who were tamei received a spark of Nadav and Avihu's soul and so felt that in their inner point they were no different from other Jews. He ties Pesach Sheni, chesed shebehod, to Lag BaOmer, hod shebehod, and teaches that no Jew becomes so tamei that it takes hold of him entirely; in the sod all Jews are equal, like the circle dance of the tzaddikim.

title.en: Why not lishmah leads to lishmah

summary.en: Returning to the Tanya, the Mashgiach asks why learning not lishmah should lead to lishmah. He answers that Hashem knows that in his inner self every Jew wants to do it lishmah, so within every act done not lishmah lies a point of lishmah, and with this every Jew can bind himself to the Torah he learns.

title.en: Torah as food, mitzvos as garments

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains the Tanya that Torah is food entering a person's inner self, while a mitzvah surrounds him like a garment. Most mitzvos relate to a particular limb, but tzitzis, sukkah and above all the spoken words of Torah surround the whole body, which is why Torah is also called a garment.

catalogTitle: תשובה על עבירות של שלש קליפות הטמאות' התיקון שבקריאת שמע בכוונה.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 7, the Mashgiach explains why sins rooted in the three impure kelipos cannot be elevated except through teshuvah out of great love, and why the Ba'al HaTanya says the sin of wasted seed can be repaired through sincere teshuvah and krias shema al hamitah.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach continues Tanya chapter 7. Permitted food eaten for pleasure rises again when the person returns to serving Hashem, though an impression stays in the body; forbidden things are bound by the kelipos until evil is uprooted in the days of Moshiach, as happened for one night at Yetzias Mitzrayim. Only teshuvah from the depth of the heart, with great love and longing, turns sins into merits and uproots them now. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on bochurim spoiled by dishonest food, explains why a ba'al teshuvah stands higher than a tzaddik, tells of a former air-force pilot who became a ba'al teshuvah, and shows the same principle in the gedolim of Eretz Yisrael who came from abroad. Finally he explains the Ba'al HaTanya's chiddush that wasted seed, though the worst sin, is easier to repair, through krias shema al hamitah, and why the Torah does not state it as an explicit prohibition.

en: Permitted food eaten for pleasure rises again with the person when he returns to serving Hashem, but an impression of it stays in the body.
Forbidden things come from the three impure kelipos and stay bound there until evil is uprooted in the days of Moshiach.
Teshuvah from the depth of the heart, with great love and longing for Hashem, turns sins into merits and uproots evil even now.
A ba'al teshuvah, having been far from Hashem, thirsts for Him more than a tzaddik and rises with greater force.
Sins become merits because they were what brought the person to his teshuvah and to his higher level.
The life-force in wasted seed, though it falls into the three impure kelipos, can rise through sincere teshuvah and krias shema al hamitah with intense kavanah.

title.en: Permitted food rises, forbidden food stays bound

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads Tanya chapter 7: permitted food eaten not for Heaven's sake rises again when the person returns to avodas Hashem, though an impression remains in the body, like a stain washed out of a garment. Forbidden things are bound by the three impure kelipos until their day comes, when Hashem slaughters the yetzer hara and death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Yetzias Mitzrayim and teshuvah from love

summary.en: The Mashgiach shows that evil was already nullified for one night at Yetzias Mitzrayim, bringing the Satmar Rav's answer on how korbanos could be taken from Egyptian animals. He then reads the Tanya that only a great teshuvah from the depth of the heart, turning sins into merits, can uproot evil from the impure kelipos now.

title.en: The Bnei Yissaschar: purifying a youth's path

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar that good bochurim who later lose their desire for Torah were fed from money not earned honestly, and remarks how hard kashrus is to guard today. The remedy, from the passuk 'with all my heart I sought You', is teshuvah with the whole heart and a longing for Hashem, which draws a light of the future and can uproot even the three impure kelipos, especially at special times.

title.en: Why a ba'al teshuvah stands higher

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that one who was far from Hashem thirsts for Him more than tzaddikim, and brings the Gemara that ba'alei teshuvah stand where tzaddikim cannot, with a mashal of a bird escaping a trap. He adds that before Moshiach all Jews will do teshuvah, and the present wave of teshuvah is the drizzle before the rain.

title.en: The pilot who became a ba'al teshuvah

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a ba'al teshuvah who had been a leading pilot in the Israeli army and now learns all day, and who sat learning on Tisha B'Av night until kiddush levana rather than go home to eat. This, he says, is the extra force of ba'alei teshuvah, who draw a breath of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: Gedolim of Eretz Yisrael from abroad

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara 'one of us is like two of them' and shows it fulfilled: since the yishuv was renewed by the talmidim of the Ba'al Shem Tov, the Gra and the Chasam Sofer, nearly all the rabbanim and gedolim of Eretz Yisrael came from abroad. He explains that one who tears himself out of the darkness of galus comes with greater longing, which is the power of teshuvah.

title.en: How sins become merits

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that sins become merits because they caused the person's teshuvah and his higher level, and uses this to explain why one who says 'I will sin and repent' is not given the chance. Teshuvah not from love brings forgiveness and turns the sins into unintentional ones, but an impression remains and the sin stays in the kelipah until death is swallowed up forever.

title.en: Krias shema al hamitah repairs wasted seed

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya that the life-force in wasted seed can rise through sincere teshuvah and intense kavanah in krias shema al hamitah, as known from the Arizal and hinted in the Gemara. Though the Shulchan Aruch calls it the worst sin, it is easier to repair; he explains that the sitra achra forms bodies from the drops, and krias shema kills them and frees the holiness.

title.en: Why the Torah does not state it as a lav

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks why the Torah mentions wasted seed only by hint, in the generation of the Flood and in Er and Onan, and answers from the Tanya that in this respect it is lighter than forbidden relations, since the life-force is not caught in a body. He contrasts the Zohar, read simply, with the Ba'al HaTanya, and explains that Hashem would not leave a Jew in a state with no way out, so the tzaddikim can give advice for its repair.

catalogTitle: Preparing for the Day when one's Spiritual Destiny is Determined

oneLiner.en: The Mashgiach explains that Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah for the Torah life of a Jew, a day of freedom, renewal and a wedding with Hashem, and that it demands more preparation than any other day of the year.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens with the Gemara that calls Shavuos a Rosh Hashanah, and with the Ramban that the Jews were not called redeemed until Matan Torah. Using a parable of a young man who thinks smoking makes him free, he shows that real freedom is release from the yetzer hara, the theme of Yovel and of the fiftieth day. Every Yom Tov is a reliving, not a commemoration, so on Shavuos the heavens open again, as a son of the Sanzer Rav saw. Hence the long preparation: Sefirah, teshuvah, the mikveh, the night of learning, even Akdamus. Shavuos is a day to become a new Jew, like Yisro and Rus. The Shabbos before feeds the Yom Tov. Shavuos is a chuppah: one must not sleep through it, the night's Tanach adorns the kallah, and the morning mikveh carries great holiness. He closes that Shavuos is a decisive day and a meeting with Hashem.

en: Shavuos is a Rosh Hashanah, and the Mashgiach says one should treat it as a new start.
True freedom is not doing whatever one wants but being free of the yetzer hara; that freedom came on the fiftieth day, with the Torah.
A Yom Tov is not a commemoration like the Fourth of July; the original event returns each year on its day.
No event in the year requires as much preparation as Shavuos: Sefirah, teshuvah, removing every barrier, the night of learning, the davening and Akdamus.
Shavuos is the chuppah between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and after all the preparation one must not miss the chuppah itself by sleeping through the davening and the reading of the Torah.
Shavuos is a decisive day on which a person receives the Torah and his avodah for the whole year.

title.en: Shavuos as a Rosh Hashanah

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Gemara that calls Shavuos a Rosh Hashanah and says one should start anew. He notes that the Jews went through a complete change between Mitzrayim and Matan Torah, and cites the Ramban that they were not called redeemed until they received the Torah.

title.en: Freedom from the yetzer hara

summary.en: Through a parable of an eighteen-year-old who buys cigarettes to show he is free, the Mashgiach shows that such a person is a slave to his yetzer hara. He ties true freedom to the luchos in Pirkei Avos, to Shemitah and Yovel, and to the fiftieth day of Sefirah, when the Jews became free servants of Hashem.

title.en: A Yom Tov is relived, not commemorated

summary.en: The Mashgiach compares the year to a rotating card file of 365 cards: what happened on a day is engraved on its card and returns with it. Unlike the Fourth of July, which only commemorates, the fifteenth of Nisan and Shavuos bring back their original light.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav's son sees Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach tells of a son of the Sanzer Rav who traveled to Belz for Shavuos and saw the heavens open at the reading of the Torah, and how his father showed him the same in Sanz only after he had worked on himself. From this he says one must believe that one receives a share in the Torah on Shavuos, and must prepare through the days of Sefirah.

title.en: Teshuvah, mikveh and the night before

summary.en: The Mashgiach asks how Rashi knows that the Jews arrived at Sinai with teshuvah, and answers that one cannot come to Sinai without it, and that their unity there proves it. He describes Shavuos as a mikveh that requires removing every barrier, the night of learning, the long davening of the tzaddikim and Akdamus as one preparation after another.

title.en: Becoming a new Jew on Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach mentions a Midrash Peliah and offers a simple explanation: Shavuos is a time to turn a new leaf, as if until now one was not a Jew. He points to Yisro and Rus, both converts, and to the Yid HaKadosh of Peshischa, for whom every day was a new becoming a Jew.

title.en: The Shabbos before Shavuos

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that the six weekdays are blessed from Shabbos, and that this is why the parsha of the Yamim Tovim in Emor opens with Shabbos: each Yom Tov draws from the Shabbos before it. He urges using the Shabbos before Shavuos, and mentions the Zohar on the night of Shavuos.

title.en: Shavuos is a chuppah: don't sleep through it

summary.en: The Mashgiach describes Shavuos as the chuppah between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, citing the piyutim and the last Mishnah in Taanis. With a parable of a chassan who prepares for weeks and then stays home from his own chuppah, he criticizes staying up all night only to sleep through the davening and the reading of the Torah, and tells of a Rebbe who sent his tired chassidim to sleep so they could daven well.

title.en: The night of Tanach adorns the kallah

summary.en: The Mashgiach explains that staying up on Shavuos night comes from the Zohar: the Torah is a kallah with twenty-four ornaments, matching the twenty-four books of Tanach, as Rashi brings, and the twenty-four arrangements of the Name of Adnus. He then raises a difficulty on the Chok Yaakov about the Mishnayos in the Tikkun.

title.en: The mikveh on Shavuos morning

summary.en: The Mashgiach speaks of the great holiness of the mikveh at daybreak on Shavuos, explains that a mikveh has levels set by halachah, and tells of a holy man who could feel by touch whether a mikveh was kosher. He brings the Arizal on the Shavuos morning tevilah and says the tzaddikim sang as they went to the mikveh.

title.en: A decisive day and a meeting with Hashem

summary.en: The Mashgiach concludes that Shavuos decides a person's Torah and avodah for the year. He brings the Chiddushei HaRim that Moshe taught the Jews the content of each Yom Tov, and explains that every regel, and Shavuos most of all, is a meeting with Hashem, for which one must come prepared and dressed in mitzvos.

catalogTitle: למצוא בדברי רשות נקודת אלקות' להשתמש בדברים גשמיים לשם שמים.

oneLiner.en: On Tanya chapter 7, the Mashgiach explains that permitted worldly things come from kelipas nogah and that a Jew can raise them to holiness by using them for the sake of Heaven, as Yitzchak found living water in the wells he dug.

abstract.en: The Mashgiach opens chapter 7 of Tanya: after showing that Torah and mitzvos clothe a person in holiness and sins clothe him in the sitra achra, the Alter Rebbe turns to permitted things. The animal soul of a Jew, kosher animals and permitted food come from kelipas nogah, a middle level that can tip either way. Eating, drinking and business are neutral in themselves; done for the sake of Heaven they rise to holiness, done for pleasure they fall to the kelipos. The world was created with the Torah, so every thing holds a point of G-dliness, and this is what Yitzchak's wells and Yaakov's sheep mean. Only a Jew can raise nogah. A plain person needs some pleasure, but with a measure each must judge for himself, as the Bnei Yissaschar explains. Pleasure taken for its own sake leaves a residue that needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound until the end of days.

en: The animal soul of a Jew comes from kelipas nogah, not from the three wholly impure kelipos, so the permitted things it uses can be turned to holiness.
A permitted thing is neutral in itself; whether it rises to holiness or falls to the kelipos depends on whether it is done for the sake of Heaven.
Since the world was created with the Torah, every thing in it holds a point of G-dliness, and a Jew came into the world to find it.
Only a Jew can raise kelipas nogah; for a non-Jew everything belongs to the three impure kelipos.
A plain person needs some pleasure from this world in order to learn and daven, but it must be taken with a measure that each one judges for himself.

Permitted food eaten for pleasure falls temporarily into the impure kelipos but can rise again when its strength is used for Torah and tefillah; its residue needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound until the end of days.

title.en: Permitted things and kelipas nogah

summary.en: The Mashgiach recalls the previous chapter, where Torah and mitzvos clothe a person in holiness and sins in the sitra achra, and introduces chapter 7 on permitted things. The animal soul of a Jew is from kelipas nogah, so permitted things are neutral and depend on intent, which he shows with matzah, chametz and bread with butter.

title.en: The Tanya text: a middle level in a mostly evil world

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya: the vital soul of a Jew, kosher animals and permitted plants, and every permitted deed, word and thought not done for Heaven draw their life from kelipas nogah. He explains nogah as a middle level, like a scale that can tip either way, and shows that this world is mostly evil with a little good mixed in.

title.en: Yitzchak's wells: finding G-dliness in the earth

summary.en: The Mashgiach applies the idea to eating and business done to serve Hashem, then turns to the parsha's account of Yitzchak's wells. Since the world was created with the Torah, the world is the composition and the Torah its commentary, and digging wells means finding the point of G-dliness in earthly things; he connects the three wells to weekday and Shabbos.

title.en: Yaakov's sheep and Yitzchak's blessing

summary.en: The Mashgiach contrasts a modern biography with the Torah's account of Yaakov tending sheep for twenty years; only one who learns with emunah knows these were not plain dealings. Yitzchak's wells were dug for all of Klal Yisroel, and his blessing of dew, fat of the land, grain and wine shows the Avos could enter material things and raise the holy sparks in them.

title.en: Business for Heaven; only a Jew raises nogah

summary.en: Citing seforim on Noach and Vayetzei, the Mashgiach says that business done in holiness, honestly and to have money for Torah, mitzvos and tzedakah, raises kelipas nogah and can reach great heights. Only a Jew can do this; he brings the Midrash that a non-Jew offers only olos, while a Jew can eat shelamim for the sake of Heaven.

title.en: A person needs pleasure, with a measure

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya on eating fat meat and drinking wine to broaden the mind for Hashem and His Torah, and explains that a plain person who is hungry cannot learn or daven. He tells of a psychologist's example of feeding through a zipper and of Rebbe Nachum of Chernobyl, and concludes that great tzaddikim aside, one must take pleasure with a measure.

title.en: Kedoshim tihyu, oneg Shabbos and Rabbah's joke

summary.en: The Mashgiach brings the Bnei Yissaschar on kedoshim tihyu and the Ramban's 'naval birshus haTorah': the Torah cannot fix how much to eat because people differ, so each must judge for himself. He adds that on Shabbos the pleasure itself is the mitzvah, and explains Rabbah's joke before the shiur as bringing the students into a good mood so the joke was absorbed into holiness.

title.en: Pleasure for its own sake, chibut hakever and forbidden things

summary.en: The Mashgiach reads the Tanya: one who eats only for pleasure brings the food's vitality down temporarily into the three impure kelipos, but because it was kosher it rises again when he learns and davens with its strength. The imprint of the pleasure remains and needs chibut hakever, while forbidden things stay bound to the kelipos until the end of days when death and impurity are removed.
